title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code, frozen outputs, and reproduction instructions: this https URL
summary: Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface.

AI.tldr: The paper asks when a reviewer agent in a multi-agent LLM system should have binding authority, and shows that an evidence gate requiring a valid violation record and a compliant repair keeps most repairs while greatly reducing corruption of correct proposals.
AI.motivation: Adding a reviewer to a multi-agent LLM system can repair errors, but a reviewer with broad override authority can also replace decisions that were already correct, and existing designs do not separate these cases.
AI.method: Compares broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair, and adds a prospective variant where the reviewer may retain, replace or escalate, tested with two open-weight models (Qwen and Mistral).
AI.result: Across 96 spatial-policy tasks and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations; in the prospective validation the retain, replace or escalate option eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals, and Qwen declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts.
AI.conclusion: Reviewer competence, action interface and binding jurisdiction jointly determine the correction domain and the corruption surface, and interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard.

title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not. We call this gap operational blindness. We introduce Agent Harness Awareness, a trust-separated design in which the host supplies a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action while retaining measurement, enforcement, evaluation, and final dispatch authority. We test its tools-and-network instance with ToolRoute, a controlled isolation benchmark that holds the task and candidate semantics constant and varies the operational information available to the model. In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. In a separate 27-decision end-to-end replication with live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults, verified state reduced mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms (zero excess observable operational cost) and completed the live action in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control. These studies establish the tools-and-network instance of Agent Harness Awareness: selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice. Runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery, and heterogeneous selection remain open empirical extensions of the same architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agent Harness Awareness, in which the host gives the model a small, fresh, verified tool-health snapshot before a consequential action, and shows that this sharply reduces observable operational regret in controlled and live tests.
AI.motivation: Tool descriptions do not reveal whether a tool is healthy at the moment of use, while the execution harness holds monitor, trace and failure information that the model choosing the next action lacks, a gap the authors call operational blindness.
AI.method: A trust-separated design in which the host supplies a verified state snapshot before each consequential action while keeping measurement, enforcement, evaluation and final dispatch authority, tested with the ToolRoute benchmark that holds task semantics fixed and varies the operational information, and with an end-to-end replication using live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans and Toxiproxy-injected faults.
AI.result: In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state cut mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%; in a 27-decision live replication, mean regret fell from 8,956 ms to 0 ms and the live action completed in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control.
AI.conclusion: Selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice in the tools-and-network setting, while runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery and heterogeneous selection remain open extensions of the same architecture.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to IEEE MECOM 2026, Marrakech, Morocco, 2-4 November 2026
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online method that reserves compute and bandwidth for agentic LLM pipelines at dispatch time with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and roughly halves the resource waste of a Chebyshev-bound baseline in simulation.
AI.motivation: The aggregate compute, bandwidth and latency demands of agentic pipelines are unknown at dispatch time and are heavy-tailed and non-stationary, so schedulers that need a fully known graph and edge methods that assume parametric or stationary demand models do not fit.
AI.method: Formalizes uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration, in which allocations must cover actual demand and deadlines must be met with a prescribed probability, and proposes CRO, an online algorithm that converts a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time allocations via conformal prediction.
AI.result: In simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles, CRO is the only evaluated method that meets target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels, and among coverage-feasible methods it attains the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction over execution traces gives a practical way to provision agentic pipelines with finite-sample coverage guarantees and less wasted capacity than a conservative distribution-bound approach.

title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. We propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment: an external CHALLENGER inspects the evolving reasoning trace and identifies specific factual or expertise gaps. These signals trigger targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment. On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), upfront retrieval provides little benefit, while challenge-aware in-between retrieval performs better; on a multi-specialist backbone it improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets and adds 6 percentage points over Challenger Only. Ablations indicate benefits from both retrieval timing and gap-specific query signals, and a live web-search experiment shows that the timing advantage persists across retrieval backends. For specialist recruitment, self-triggered adaptation is unreliable, whereas Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, with positive direction on all tested generalization datasets. Naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment degrades performance, highlighting the need to coordinate adaptive intervention channels. These results show that when and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes challenge-aware adaptive recruitment, in which an external Challenger inspects the evolving reasoning trace and triggers targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment for medical multi-agent reasoning.
AI.motivation: On hard medical QA, multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting because existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning.
AI.method: An external CHALLENGER identifies specific factual or expertise gaps in the evolving reasoning trace, and these signals trigger gap-specific retrieval or specialist recruitment mid-discussion, compared against upfront retrieval and self-triggered adaptation.
AI.result: On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), challenge-aware in-between retrieval outperforms upfront retrieval and improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets with a multi-specialist backbone, adding 6 percentage points over Challenger Only; Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, while naively combining retrieval and recruitment degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: When and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning, and the adaptive intervention channels must be coordinated rather than simply stacked.

title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
summary: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a closed-form feasibility condition that tells when no confidence threshold makes a tiered LLM cascade worthwhile compared with sending every query to the backstop model, and shows how this answer inverts along the architecture cost ratio kappa.
AI.motivation: Tiered inference routes queries between on-device or edge models and datacenter models using confidence signals from frozen checkpoints, but there has been no principled test of whether such a cascade can be worthwhile at all.
AI.method: Models the routing decision as a binary test and separates local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio kappa, deriving a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor and a perfect-signal ceiling.
AI.result: Below the signal-free floor a cascade is feasible at any signal quality and above the perfect-signal ceiling none is; where local compute is billed, cost binds, whereas where it is sunk, as on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead determines what the cascade achieves.
AI.conclusion: The condition and its inversion hold independently of any particular architecture and form the paper's contribution, and the authors reduce them to three design requirements that existing primitives satisfy only in isolation, leaving a co-designed architecture as future work.

title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
summary: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReScopeBench, a benchmark of 18 interactive environments for the experience lifecycle of agents, and finds that retained experience improves task performance but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks study experience reuse and adaptation but give limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain or lose as environments evolve.
AI.method: Separates structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints, and uses an experience-first construction that builds task streams around shared experience and injects silent environmental changes while tracking saved experience throughout each stream.
AI.result: Across 20 models, retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change, and even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully.
AI.conclusion: Selective maintenance of experience and its effective use are complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Data, prompts, analysis scripts and results: this https URL (GitHub: this https URL)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus. In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review. No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates six AI tools across the stages of a literature review on the Spanish plume weather pattern, finding that they help with discovery and interpretation but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence.
AI.motivation: LLM evaluations usually test individual tasks rather than the whole review process, so the authors assess the end-to-end workflow against a published review of the Spanish plume and its 102-article corpus.
AI.method: Tests six AI tools across four stages (finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them and proposing future research), with syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts.
AI.result: Five tools collectively identified 57 articles and the best single tool found 42; institutional library access raised discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code; three tools identified all 18 substantial articles but misclassified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial, and their syntheses were largely accurate but sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors and exaggerated consensus.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly with institutional access, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research, and the authors offer eight recommendations for researchers.

title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
summary: AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. Even simple workplace questions may require locating relevant channels and direct messages, recovering context from long discussions, inspecting repository state, reconciling stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesizing across sources. We introduce SlackBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that require joint reasoning over workplace communication and evolving repository state. Grounded in privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic research projects, SlackBench provides reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions, and corresponding code changes grounded in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. It contains 140 queries spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference over long conversations. These tasks are not reducible to static corpus question answering: agents must determine which conversations matter, traverse threads, inspect repository state, and synthesize evidence across communication and code artifacts. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%, highlighting substantial headroom for improvement. SlackBench thus provides an extensible framework for evaluating agents in collaborative work environments. The SlackBench dataset is available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SlackBench, a benchmark of 140 queries over privacy-preserving reenactments of real research projects that require agents to reason jointly over workplace communication and evolving GitHub repositories and Google Docs, with the best system scoring around 80%.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks and miss the multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code and evolving decisions.
AI.method: Builds reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions and matching code changes grounded in GitHub and Google Docs, with queries covering heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization and circumstance inference over long conversations.
AI.result: Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark shows substantial headroom for agents in collaborative work settings, and because its tasks cannot be reduced to static corpus question answering it provides an extensible framework for evaluating them.

title: MA-SafeDiffuser: Safe Multi-Agent Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
comment: Accepted at AAMAS 2026. 14 pages, including supplementary material
summary: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that gives diffusion-based trajectory planners finite-time invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety, and reduces safety violations relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Diffusion trajectory planners lack guarantees for joint safety among several agents, and single-agent constructions do not cover pairwise constraints or the local-trap and deadlock phenomena that arise in multi-agent settings.
AI.method: Formalizes joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets, derives centralized and decentralized communication-aware constrained denoising procedures that embed control barrier function constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, handles deadlock with time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs, and adds a multi-agent Maze2D benchmarking suite.
AI.result: Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines while retaining planning quality.
AI.conclusion: The method comes with provable invariance under mild assumptions, together with algorithms, proofs and reference implementations for safe multi-agent planning with diffusion models.

title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
summary: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware non-autoregressive framework for whole-page ranking that approaches autoregressive generation quality at much lower inference cost and improves engagement in a live social-video test.
AI.motivation: Non-autoregressive page ranking scores each item independently and misses order-dependent interactions, while autoregressive methods capture those interactions but add inference overhead that is hard to deploy at industrial scale.
AI.method: Computes reusable representations once per request and performs lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, integrating global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning and position-aware scoring in a shared representation architecture.
AI.result: On KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS, MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while decoding 4.07x and 3.54x faster on CPU; in a randomized evaluation on a large social-video platform it improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058% while cutting ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%.
AI.conclusion: Prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between non-autoregressive and autoregressive generation while retaining the efficiency that industrial scalability requires.

title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
summary: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and this http URL. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that writer-grader loops over end-to-end data science projects raise the average score from 59% to 76% over three rounds, but the gain depends on which model plays which role, and weaker models generally do not improve stronger ones.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how far agentic models can complete an end-to-end data science project and how much feedback helps, including whether a model grading its own work is biased and whether extra revision budget alone matters.
AI.method: A writer model with tools downloads, cleans and analyzes a dataset and writes a short paper; the project is executed and a grader model scores it, and the writer revises over three rounds, with seven models from five developers each acting as writer and grader in 49 pairs, each run three times.
AI.result: Of 147 initial submissions, 107 ran and rendered, and the average score rose from 59% to 76% after the final round; by writer the gain ranged from 3 points for Opus 5.5 to 46 points for Haiku 4.5, and by grader from 13 to 32 points; self-grading scored about 9 points higher than the average of the other models' grades, and about half of the round-to-round difference lay within grader noise.
AI.conclusion: How much the revision loop helps depends on which model plays which role, and weaker models generally do not improve stronger models, while revision without feedback helps some models but not others.

title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
summary: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.

AI.tldr: A global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders and policymakers, complemented by an end-user focus group, finds that the three groups share a view of transparency but that the gap between desired and available transparency is largest for end-users.
AI.motivation: Transparency is a central principle of AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what it means, for whom and in what contexts, and the group most underserved by current practice has been poorly represented.
AI.method: Draws on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, combining a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders and policymakers with a structured focus group of end-users.
AI.result: All three groups centre transparency on accuracy and privacy; only 28% of end-users say current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared with 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers; transparency priorities shift with context and task structure.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful AI transparency requires pluralistic transparency infrastructures that go beyond one-size-fits-all disclosure and static documentation.

title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
summary: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates operationalization of virtual-trial protocols on routinely collected clinical data by selecting reusable procedural skills per stage and enforcing explicit contracts, reaching 95.1% reference-matched workflows.
AI.motivation: Translating a study protocol into an executable analysis on routinely collected clinical data requires consistent decisions about source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage and timing, and these decisions depend on local data representations and conventions.
AI.method: Selects reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to keep study decisions consistent across stages, and introduces VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction.
AI.result: Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus; procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and raised source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases; site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions improves virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas, and the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program.

title: AGORA: Reliability-Aware Aggregation of LLM Judges via Item-Response Theory
summary: LLM-as-a-judge is a common substitute for costly human evaluation, and aggregating several judges is the standard remedy for any single judge's bias. Judge pools mix judges of very different reliability, while the human-labeled sets that validate them hold a few hundred items or fewer. In this regime the per-item mean weights weak judges as heavily as strong ones, and confusion-table models such as Dawid-Skene must estimate a per-judge error table from too few items. We propose AGORA (Aggregation Of Reliability-weighted Assessments), an item-response-theory aggregator that places every item on one latent quality scale and describes each judge by a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, so judge reliability is learned from all items jointly and without human labels. Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items. It remains accurate as pools grow more uneven, a label-free dispersion statistic indicates in advance when trust weighting helps, and its learned trust weights track per-judge human validity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AGORA, an item-response-theory aggregator that combines LLM judges using reliability weights learned without human labels, matching or exceeding Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets and gaining the most as the validation set shrinks.
AI.motivation: Judge pools mix judges of very different reliability while the human-labeled validation sets hold only a few hundred items or fewer, so per-item means over-weight weak judges and confusion-table models such as Dawid-Skene cannot estimate per-judge error tables reliably.
AI.method: Places every item on one latent quality scale and describes each judge by a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, so that judge reliability is learned from all items jointly without human labels.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items; it stays accurate as judge pools grow more uneven, and its learned trust weights track per-judge human validity.
AI.conclusion: A label-free dispersion statistic indicates in advance when trust weighting will help, which makes reliability-aware aggregation a practical choice for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation with small validation sets.

title: BrainBind: Bridging Synchronized EEG and fMRI through Long-Form Naturalistic Video Representations
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026. 26 pages, 4 figures, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: Real-world vision is dynamic and scene-rich, while EEG and fMRI resolve it at complementary temporal and spatial scales. Most neural decoding systems, however, align one modality in isolation and mostly against static images or short clips. We study the synchronized case: EEG and fMRI are recorded during the same long-form naturalistic viewing, giving a shared stimulus but also recurring narrative context and many semantically similar candidates. We present BrainBind, a framework that maps synchronized EEG and fMRI into frozen long-form video embedding spaces and treats those spaces as common visual-semantic references, not literal neural codes. On CineBrain, a five-seed Recall@K 2 x 4 matrix across two video anchors and four system configurations shows distinct retrieval profiles. With Omni, fMRI organizes the full candidate list most strongly (MRR = 23.82, nDCG@10 = 25.31), while Joint-Dual gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%) with a distinct rank-wide profile. The complementary episode-disjoint evaluation quantifies the contribution of repeated stimulus identity and narrative context to the random split. Across these experiments, proxy choice and system configuration produce distinct top-rank and rank-wide retrieval profiles within the present synchronized dataset. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BrainBind, which maps synchronized EEG and fMRI recorded during long naturalistic video into frozen video embedding spaces and retrieves the matching clips, with distinct retrieval profiles across proxies and system configurations.
AI.motivation: Most neural decoding systems align one modality in isolation and mostly against static images or short clips, leaving synchronized EEG and fMRI recorded during long-form naturalistic viewing largely unexplored.
AI.method: Maps EEG and fMRI into frozen long-form video embedding spaces that serve as common visual-semantic references rather than literal neural codes, evaluated on CineBrain with a five-seed Recall@K matrix across two video anchors and four system configurations, plus an episode-disjoint evaluation.
AI.result: With Omni, fMRI organizes the full candidate list most strongly (MRR 23.82, nDCG@10 25.31), while Joint-Dual gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%) with a distinct rank-wide profile; the episode-disjoint evaluation quantifies how much repeated stimulus identity and narrative context contribute to the random split.
AI.conclusion: Proxy choice and system configuration produce distinct top-rank and rank-wide retrieval profiles within this synchronized dataset, so both the reference space and the configuration matter for retrieval.

title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system
summary: As autonomous AI agents enter permissionless onchain markets, selecting new service providers remains a core challenge. Existing reputation systems depend on scarce resources like human curation, identity credentials, or voluntary reviews, while naive volume rankings are vulnerable to Sybil attacks. We evaluate whether existing onchain payment histories can yield provider ratings that are resilient against Sybil attacks. Using a 157-day dataset comprising 66M agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains, we model payment flows as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers. A provider's rating is derived from graph paths linked to a buyer's existing trusted network. We propose three Sybil-resistant rating algorithms: a max-flow rating and two relaxed algorithms optimized for stronger rating performance. Evaluating these algorithms against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers, we show that rating manipulation costs 20% of those buyers' total spend and is around 23x harder to manipulate than the standard similarity rule (collaborative filtering).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes three Sybil-resistant rating algorithms for service providers in an agentic onchain marketplace, built on payment graphs, and shows that manipulating a rating costs 20% of a buyer's total spend and is about 23x harder than the standard collaborative-filtering similarity rule.
AI.motivation: Selecting new service providers in permissionless onchain agent markets relies on scarce resources such as human curation, identity credentials or voluntary reviews, while naive volume rankings are vulnerable to Sybil attacks.
AI.method: Models 157 days of data comprising 66M agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers, derives a provider's rating from graph paths linked to a buyer's existing trusted network using a max-flow rating and two relaxed algorithms, and evaluates them against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers.
AI.result: Rating manipulation costs 20% of those buyers' total spend and is around 23x harder to manipulate than the standard similarity rule (collaborative filtering).
AI.conclusion: Existing onchain payment histories can yield provider ratings that resist Sybil attacks without depending on identity credentials, human curation or voluntary reviews.

title: Verified but Vacuous: Three Failure Surfaces of LLM-Driven Verified Code Generation
summary: What should ``verified'' mean when evaluating LLM-generated code? Many existing pipelines report a single verification number. We argue this collapses three distinct properties measured in a conditional audit sequence: verifier acceptance (Surface A), \emph{syntactic specification binding (Surface B: does the proof obligation bind to the spec?), and \emph{semantic specification fidelity} (Surface C: does the spec capture the informal requirement?). Two empirical demonstrations show the surfaces separate. \textbf{First ($A \neq B$), via Li@Opus (a same-model reproduction of \citet{li2025dafny}'s Dafny-as-intermediate-representation (IR) pipeline under Claude Opus 4.7) on three Python benchmarks}: it reaches \textbf{99.1\% verifier acceptance} on HumanEval while only \textbf{1.9\%} carry a certificate binding to a spec-defined predicate or function. \textbf{Second ($B \neq C$), via VCG on two Rust benchmarks}: we use VCG (which is our own in-house Dafny-as-intermediate pipeline) on Rust because the Rust target lets us enforce fully-verifiable output (every component ships as a Dafny certificate, ensures-binding gate passing by construction). Even inside that construction, \textbf{11.48\% (MBPP-Rust) and 14.82\% (VeriContest LC slice) of structurally-verified samples still fail hidden tests}. On the LC slice of VeriContest, \textbf{VCG's reported End2End rate is 7.79\% (535/6870).} The cited external rates are 5.51\% (GPT-5.5) and 1.88\% (single-shot Opus 4.7). These give descriptive differences of 2.3 percentage points and 4.14$\times$, respectively; task-budget, repair and harness differences prevent a matched-performance claim.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a single verification number for LLM-generated code hides three distinct properties, and shows with two demonstrations that verifier acceptance, syntactic specification binding and semantic specification fidelity can separate in practice.
AI.motivation: Many pipelines report one verification figure for LLM-generated code, which collapses verifier acceptance, whether the proof obligation binds to the spec, and whether the spec captures the informal requirement.
AI.method: Defines a conditional audit sequence with three surfaces (A: verifier acceptance, B: syntactic specification binding, C: semantic specification fidelity), tests A against B with a same-model reproduction of a Dafny-as-intermediate-representation pipeline under Claude Opus 4.7 on three Python benchmarks, and tests B against C with the VCG pipeline on two Rust benchmarks.
AI.result: The Li@Opus reproduction reaches 99.1% verifier acceptance on HumanEval while only 1.9% of outputs carry a certificate binding to a spec-defined predicate or function; on Rust, 11.48% (MBPP-Rust) and 14.82% (VeriContest LC slice) of structurally verified samples still fail hidden tests; VCG's End2End rate on the LC slice is 7.79% (535/6870), against cited external rates of 5.51% (GPT-5.5) and 1.88% (single-shot Opus 4.7), descriptive differences that do not support a matched-performance claim.
AI.conclusion: Verification claims for LLM-generated code should report the three surfaces separately, because verifier acceptance alone overstates correctness.

title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
summary: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Hybrid Spark, a speculative decoding framework that runs a model-based drafter and a model-free n-gram drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, improving output throughput on code editing while matching it on chat.
AI.motivation: The gain from speculative decoding depends on workload shape and content, and model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in adaptive verification budget allocation, which forces deployments to fix one drafter or split GPUs between drafters.
AI.method: Runs both drafters at every step and uses a price per verified draft token, the goodput that the slot would earn elsewhere in the batch, after calibrating the n-gram drafter's acceptance estimates once on general text so that both chains sit on one scale; implemented with Dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, entirely on the GPU, keeping asynchronous scheduling intact.
AI.result: Hybrid Spark achieves 1.10 to 1.62x the output throughput of Dspark on code editing at batch size 4 and 1.04 to 1.27x at batch size 128, while staying at 0.97 to 1.01x of it on chat at temperature 0.
AI.conclusion: A single deployment can therefore serve both code-editing and chat workloads without fixing one drafter or splitting GPUs between drafters.

title: ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building
summary: On Replit, our agentic engineering platform, users now build entire products without writing code, through successive feature requests to an agent. Yet existing coding benchmarks evaluate single, fully specified tasks, and many are near saturation. We introduce ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software building that we use to select our platform's models. Its 17 full-stack web products, modeled on widely used software, grow over 241 feature requests and are judged only when finished, as a user would judge them: a browser agent runs 544 test plans, and a build passes only if every plan does, under a grading protocol validated to keep this strict score reliable. Evaluating nine models, we find a reliability gap: the three strongest pass up to 98% of test plans yet deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds, and no open-weight model delivers one. The gap is closing fast: across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rises from 3% to 53% while the cost per build falls by more than half. We release eight products with the harness and grader, hold out nine, and report lessons from production use.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software building with 17 full-stack web products and 241 feature requests, and finds that the strongest models pass most test plans yet rarely deliver a fully working product.
AI.motivation: Users now build whole products through successive feature requests to an agent, but existing coding benchmarks evaluate single fully specified tasks and many are near saturation.
AI.method: Grows 17 full-stack web products through 241 feature requests and judges each build only when it is finished, using a browser agent that runs 544 test plans, where a build passes only if every plan does, under a grading protocol validated for reliability; nine models were evaluated, eight products are released with the harness and grader, and nine are held out.
AI.result: The three strongest models pass up to 98% of test plans yet deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds, and no open-weight model delivers one; across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rises from 3% to 53% while cost per build falls by more than half.
AI.conclusion: A reliability gap remains between passing individual test plans and delivering a complete product, but it is closing fast, and the authors report lessons from production use.

title: Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Autonomous software agents can act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight. We present Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), an approach designed to be harness-independent, for maintaining operational authority according to currently justified assurance. It distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, and resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy. A typed dependency graph supports selective re-evaluation of authorization-relevant changes. An authority epoch changes when effective authority changes; a distinct optional authorization-basis version supports revalidation of action-specific authorization conditions. Protected effect-time enforcement can reject stale actions before a consequential resource change, subject to the available commit mechanism. A compositional Domain Governance Profile expresses domain-specific semantics without granting authority. Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response, and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary. The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), a harness-independent approach that keeps an autonomous agent's operational authority matched to its currently justified assurance, with a trading-domain regression suite demonstrating contraction, recovery and stale-action rejection.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight, so an authorization can outlive the evidence that justified it.
AI.method: Distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy, uses a typed dependency graph for selective re-evaluation, marks authority changes with an authority epoch and a separate basis version, enforces protected effect-time checks, and adds a compositional Domain Governance Profile.
AI.result: Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain only, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.

title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents
summary: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper makes weight memory, which stores facts in model parameters, competitive with text memory for long-term factual recall, using on-policy self-distillation and a verify-then-regenerate router that chooses between weight and text memory per query. On HaluMem it matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines while reading fewer tokens per query.
AI.motivation: Text-based agent memory extracts key points and retrieves them into context at query time, so each query's cost grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory avoids this but has been explored mainly for skills and behaviors rather than episodic and semantic facts, and it lags text systems in recall.
AI.method: The authors apply on-policy self-distillation, training a context-free student from a teacher that is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router so that weight memory and text memory each cover the queries they handle best.
AI.result: On the HaluMem benchmark, the approach matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. An extensive study characterizes the behavior of weight memory and how different training recipes affect its performance.
AI.conclusion: Weight memory, combined with retrieval, is positioned as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory for persistent multi-session deployments, with insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols.

title: Attributing Agent Failures to Their History Needs an Executed Counterfactual: Toward a Reporting Standard
comment: Accepted at the IAB Workshop (Interpreting Agent Behavior) at NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 20 pages
summary: Published explanations of why long-horizon agents fail are commonly taxonomies labeled over completed trajectories: a judge reads a transcript and names the failure. We argue that a claim attributing an agent's behavior to its history should carry intervention-verified evidence, per instance or via a validated estimator: freeze an executable mid-trajectory state, alter only the history the agent sees, and continue - executed rather than inferred from the transcript, at a state whose restoration has been measured, with a replay certificate matched to the estimand. Each of the four manipulation classes we name has a precedent, and several methods already execute interventions from checkpoints, re-executed prefixes or recorded conversation states (for example DoVer, REFLECT, Min et al., Who&When Pro, Causal Agent Replay), but none reports a measured replay certificate. Two cautionary measurements, neither applying the standard, follow: a carrier taxonomy whose "concentration" could not be separated from benchmark construction (adjusted odds ratio 1.15, interval crossing 1), and hash-identical snapshots that, restored into identically seeded processes, agreed with one another in 24 of 24 states while differing from the live continuation in 9 and 20 of 24. Restoring the captured position of a random stream made all 24 agree with the live run.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that claims attributing an agent's behavior to its history should rest on executed, intervention-verified counterfactuals rather than judgments over transcripts, and proposes a reporting standard built on measured replay certificates. Two cautionary measurements show that restored snapshots can agree with one another while diverging from the live run.
AI.motivation: Published explanations of long-horizon agent failures are usually taxonomies labeled by a judge reading completed transcripts, which infers causes instead of testing them. Existing intervention methods do not report a measured replay certificate.
AI.method: The proposed standard requires freezing an executable mid-trajectory state, altering only the history the agent sees, and continuing execution, at a state whose restoration has been measured, with a replay certificate matched to the estimand. The paper names four manipulation classes, each with a precedent in prior methods such as DoVer, REFLECT and Causal Agent Replay.
AI.result: A carrier taxonomy's concentration could not be separated from benchmark construction (adjusted odds ratio 1.15, interval crossing 1). Hash-identical snapshots restored into identically seeded processes agreed with one another in 24 of 24 states, yet differed from the live continuation in 9 and 20 of 24 states. Restoring the captured position of a random stream made all 24 agree with the live run.
AI.conclusion: Intervention-verified evidence with measured replay certificates is proposed as the reporting standard for attributing agent behavior to its history, and the measurements show that restored replays can silently diverge from live runs unless the random stream position is also restored.

title: Quantifying Trait-State Hierarchy in EEG Foundation Model and Signal Processing Embeddings
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) measures brain activity through recording electrical potentials of the scalp. EEG recordings capture two distinct sets of characteristics in the signal: (1) \emph{Traits} -- information that remains relatively constant over the course of a recording session, such as subject identity, age, and sex; (2) \emph{States} -- signatures that encode responses to external stimuli, including visual, auditory, and motor information. There is limited understanding of how different EEG modeling features (signal processing and foundation models) encode state and trait characteristics. In this work, we quantify state- and trait-level features captured by EEG embeddings using a hierarchy metric and kNN purity on Brain-Computer Interface dataset trials, and find that a majority of EEG features form a macro-trait hierarchy (embeddings form trait-level clusters with micro-states within). Our linear probe results indicate that this hierarchy structure leads to suboptimal state distinguishability, negatively impacting BCI performance of EEG foundation models. To mitigate this, we explore normalization techniques that reduce trait-specific information in embeddings and provide a $\sim$ 10\% improvement in balanced accuracy for state classification. Additionally, we observe that when fine-tuning models for downstream state decoding, embedding spaces transform from macro-trait to macro-state hierarchies, which in turn lead to better state decoding.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how EEG embeddings from signal-processing features and foundation models encode traits, which stay stable across a session, versus states, which respond to stimuli. Most features form a trait-dominated hierarchy that hurts state decoding, and normalization and fine-tuning can reduce this effect.
AI.motivation: EEG recordings mix session-stable traits such as subject identity, age and sex with stimulus-driven states, but how different EEG modeling features encode each is poorly understood, and trait structure may hurt BCI performance.
AI.method: The authors measure state- and trait-level structure of EEG embeddings with a hierarchy metric and kNN purity on BCI dataset trials, use linear probes to assess state distinguishability, and explore normalization techniques that reduce trait-specific information in the embeddings.
AI.result: A majority of EEG features form a macro-trait hierarchy with micro-states inside it, which gives suboptimal state distinguishability. Normalization gives about a 10% improvement in balanced accuracy for state classification. When models are fine-tuned for state decoding, embedding spaces shift from macro-trait to macro-state hierarchies, which leads to better state decoding.
AI.conclusion: Trait-dominated embedding structure limits state decoding in EEG foundation models, and reducing trait information or fine-tuning toward states improves it, pointing to trait suppression as a design consideration for BCI models.

title: Grounded but Not Immune: Confirmation Bias in Agent-as-a-judge
summary: Evaluating open-ended agent tasks increasingly falls to an Agent-as-a-Judge: an evaluator handed tools and the agent's full trajectory so it can verify a result against the environment. The premise is that a judge that gathers its own evidence should be grounded by it. We show that this grounding does not immunize the judge against confirmation bias: a single false pre-screening note, attributed to an authority and carrying no evidential bearing on the correct verdict, overturns up to 40% of a tool-using judge's correct verdicts across four judges and five datasets, even though the judge collects decisive evidence. The shift is driven by specific properties of the cue. We treat this cue as a controlled diagnostic of confirmation bias rather than an adversarial attack. Our central contribution is to explain how confirmation bias changes the judge's behavior in a trajectory. We classify changes in judge behavior and attribute changes to one of three failure modes: over-trust (verify, conclude correctly, then defer), hallucination (fabricate support for the flip), and under-investigation (stop at the first corroborating signal). For the two Claude judges, the failure is predominantly over-trust (67-75% of harmful flips), while smaller judges have error modes spread across all three. Lightweight mitigations blunt but never remove the bias.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an Agent-as-a-Judge with tools remains vulnerable to confirmation bias: one false pre-screening note with an authority attribution overturns up to 40% of a tool-using judge's correct verdicts. It classifies the resulting failures into over-trust, hallucination and under-investigation, and finds that lightweight mitigations only partly help.
AI.motivation: Agent-as-a-Judge evaluators are assumed to be grounded because they gather their own evidence from the environment, but this premise had not been tested against confirmation bias.
AI.method: The authors inject a single false pre-screening note, attributed to an authority and carrying no evidential bearing on the correct verdict, as a controlled diagnostic across four judges and five datasets. They classify changes in judge behavior and attribute them to over-trust, hallucination or under-investigation.
AI.result: The cue overturns up to 40% of correct verdicts even though the judge collects decisive evidence. For the two Claude judges, over-trust accounts for 67-75% of harmful flips, while smaller judges show error modes spread across all three failure types.
AI.conclusion: Grounding through tool use does not immunize judges against confirmation bias, and lightweight mitigations blunt the bias without removing it, so evaluators need stronger safeguards.

title: Combining Relevant Expert Knowledge Using Mixtures of Feedback Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
summary: A neuro-symbolic system should combine only relevant answers from expert agents or other knowledge sources. Using only relevant experts for a given input query becomes ever more important for accuracy and scalability as the knowledge network grows and connects ever more knowledge sources. We extend the standard definition of relevance from the legal theory of evidence: An answer is relevant if and only if it is both probative and material for the matter at hand given the knowledge available. We apply this relevancy scheme to mixing the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps (FCMs) of real or artificial experts. The expert FCM directed causal graphs mix or combine into a common knowledge network. We compare the equilibrium limit-cycle predictions or answers of the experts to the answers of the mixture FCM and then estimate the probative status of answers by their difference or variation. A new Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge mixture into corresponding posterior-like FCMs that also allow relevancy-based comparisons. The result is a final set of relevancy mixing weights that produces a relevancy-mixed FCM knowledge network for the given query. So different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs. We demonstrate this relevancy approach using generated synthetic FCMs from an actual 13-node expert FCM that models the causes and feedbacks of ischemic-stroke risk.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a relevance-based way to mix the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps of several experts, so that each query yields its own relevancy-weighted knowledge network instead of one fixed mixture. It is demonstrated on synthetic FCMs generated from a 13-node expert model of ischemic-stroke risk.
AI.motivation: As neuro-symbolic systems connect more knowledge sources, combining answers from irrelevant experts harms accuracy and scalability, so a principled notion of relevance is needed when mixing expert knowledge.
AI.method: Relevance is defined following legal evidence theory as being both probative and material. Expert FCMs are mixed into a common network, the experts' answers are compared with the mixture's answers at equilibrium limit cycles, and a Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge into posterior-like FCMs that yield relevancy mixing weights for each query.
AI.result: The abstract reports only a demonstration, using synthetic FCMs generated from an actual 13-node expert FCM of ischemic-stroke causes and feedbacks, and gives no quantitative comparison.
AI.conclusion: Relevance-weighted mixing lets different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs, offering a way to scale expert knowledge networks while keeping only the relevant answers.

title: How Do Artificial Agents Make Decisions in Light of Visual Data?
comment: Presented at the Workshop on GenAI, Agents, and the Future of VIS, held in conjunction with IEEE VIS, 2026
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how vision-language model agents perceive uncertainty in charts and make decisions from visual data. GPT-4o is the most accurate at perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models, and agents align best with rational decision theory when uncertainty is shown as circle charts, icon arrays or text.
AI.motivation: Much human knowledge is encoded visually, yet how VLM-powered agents perceive and act under uncertainty in visual data is not well understood.
AI.method: Building on visualization literacy and decision theory, the authors ran two complementary studies: one on how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and one on how agents make decisions from images. They analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types.
AI.result: GPT-4o shows the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. Agents show the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty is represented as circle charts, icon arrays or text.
AI.conclusion: The visualization format affects both the perception and the decision quality of VLM agents, so the choice of uncertainty encoding matters when agents act on visual data.

title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects
summary: Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation. We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. In turn, a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Together they constitute a complete account of individual causal effects.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that individualized causal effects are better captured by Petri nets under the individual token philosophy than by type-level structural causal models, and proposes a formal translation from Bayesian networks to Petri nets. It pairs this token-level structure with a conformal prediction layer that gives finite-sample coverage guarantees for causal effects.
