AI.motivation: Structural causal models and Bayesian networks are type-level formalisms whose estimands, the ATE and CATE, are properties of population distributions that collapse under unbounded treatment-effect heterogeneity, so they do not capture the structure of individual causation.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal translation from Bayesian networks to Petri nets, giving a two-layer account. The Petri net layer represents causal mechanisms without distributional assumptions, and a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments or quantitative results. The contribution is a formal and theoretical account, and the claim of a complete account of individual causal effects rests on that argument alone.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that Petri nets with conformal prediction together give a complete account of individualized causality, a claim the abstract supports only through the formal argument, with no empirical test reported.

title: Agents, Think Only When it Helps
summary: LLM agent distillation transfers agentic capabilities to student models by training on complete teacher trajectories that typically interleave thoughts and actions. We question how critical thought supervision is for agents' ultimate action performance. To answer this, we disentangle their impacts by independently perturbing teacher thoughts and actions during distillation. On widely adopted agent benchmarks across model scales, altering or discarding thoughts has little effect on student performance. We find, however, that thought supervision becomes important when information about the thought is not disclosed in the corresponding action during training. By identifying such discrepant cases, our findings challenge the common practice of distilling entire teacher trajectories for LLM agents, and offer a new insight that thought supervision can be a discernible choice for efficiency depending on whether the information of thought is disclosed in the action.

AI.tldr: For LLM agent distillation, perturbing or discarding teacher thoughts has little effect on student action performance across benchmarks and model scales. Thought supervision matters only when the information in a thought is not disclosed in the corresponding action during training.
AI.motivation: Distillation usually trains student agents on complete teacher trajectories that interleave thoughts and actions, but how critical thought supervision is to final action performance is unclear.
AI.method: The authors disentangle the two by independently perturbing teacher thoughts and teacher actions during distillation, and evaluate on widely adopted agent benchmarks across model scales.
AI.result: Altering or discarding thoughts has little effect on student performance. Thought supervision becomes important when the information about a thought is not disclosed in the corresponding action during training, and the paper identifies such discrepant cases.
AI.conclusion: The common practice of distilling entire teacher trajectories is challenged; thought supervision can be a deliberate efficiency choice, depending on whether the action discloses the thought's information.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Best Paper Award at the SEPH 2026 workshop, UbiComp Companion '26
summary: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

AI.tldr: Self-supervised masked-autoencoder pretraining of a Vision Transformer on unlabelled optomyographic smart-glasses recordings improves five-class facial expression recognition. With only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms a from-scratch model trained on all labels.
AI.motivation: Facial expression recognition on privacy-preserving smart glasses such as OCOsense needs labelled data that is costly to collect, and fully supervised systems limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings.
AI.method: A Vision Transformer is pretrained with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and then finetuned for five-class facial expression recognition under person-independent cross-validation.
AI.result: Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance. With 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart-eyewear expression recognition, with implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions
summary: Coding agents must deliver correct software while respecting users' expertise, preferences, and working conditions. Existing benchmarks increasingly incorporate interaction, yet personalized requirement fulfillment remains underexplored. We introduce PersonaCodeBench, which turns user characteristics into verifiable obligations in persona-driven multi-turn coding sessions. Our persona pool spans roles, technical abilities, interaction preferences, and practical constraints, yielding task-grounded evolved requirements for implementation, permissions, testing, explanation, and delivery. At runtime, a controller governs user simulator responses and requirement disclosure, using online requirement evaluation to provide feedback and advance the interaction. Requirements emerge progressively, with their content, disclosure conditions, and acceptance criteria fixed before evaluation. A completion verifier and a personalization verifier separately assess native correctness and persona fulfillment. Joint pass requires both adherence to the declared budget and compliance with validity conditions. We evaluate all major frontier agents, establish a comprehensive leaderboard, and conduct detailed experimental analyses to validate effectiveness. PersonaCodeBench supports reproducible evaluation of coding agents' ability to meet explicit, personalized user expectations alongside coding objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PersonaCodeBench, a benchmark that turns user personas into verifiable requirements in multi-turn coding sessions, testing whether coding agents meet both correctness and personalized expectations. A joint pass requires adherence to the declared budget as well as satisfaction of the persona requirements.
AI.motivation: Coding agents must respect users' expertise, preferences and working conditions, but existing interactive benchmarks rarely evaluate personalized requirement fulfillment.
AI.method: Persona pools span roles, technical abilities, interaction preferences and practical constraints, yielding task-grounded requirements for implementation, permissions, testing, explanation and delivery. A controller governs user-simulator responses and requirement disclosure, using online requirement evaluation. A completion verifier and a personalization verifier assess native correctness and persona fulfillment separately.
AI.result: The abstract reports that all major frontier agents were evaluated and placed on a comprehensive leaderboard, with detailed experimental analyses, but it gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: PersonaCodeBench supports reproducible evaluation of whether coding agents meet explicit, personalized user expectations alongside their coding objectives.

title: Toward a Compositional Knowledge Architecture for a Shared Organizational Cortex
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Evaluation and sources in this https URL (tag registered-plan)
summary: Organizations accumulate evidence in conversations, documents, decisions and relationships, but they act on interpretations: judgements assembled from several observations, resting on assumptions, and revised as circumstances change. Existing retrieval, knowledge graphs and agent memory keep the records and lose the interpretation. We propose a four-layer architecture, Signals, Domains, Claims and Dimensions, in which interpretations persist with their justifications and standing, a truth-maintenance network revises that standing as evidence changes, and validated, versioned Dimensions position interpretations on named axes. We call the result a shared organizational cortex. In a registered retrieval experiment, the Dimension term gains 0.028 nDCG@10 (p = 0.002). In system-level comparisons, the full retrieval configuration improves nDCG@10 by 0.081 over Signals-only and 0.053 over graph-augmented Signals-only retrieval (both reported p < 0.001). The architecture gives organizations a persistent, revisable basis for shared judgement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a four-layer architecture, Signals, Domains, Claims and Dimensions, in which organizational interpretations persist with their justifications and are revised by a truth-maintenance network as evidence changes. In a registered retrieval experiment, the Dimension term gains 0.028 nDCG@10 (p = 0.002), and the full configuration improves nDCG@10 by 0.081 over Signals-only retrieval.
AI.motivation: Organizations act on interpretations assembled from observations and assumptions, but retrieval, knowledge graphs and agent memory keep the records and lose the interpretation.
AI.method: Interpretations are stored with their justifications and standing across the four layers, a truth-maintenance network revises their standing as evidence changes, and validated, versioned Dimensions place interpretations on named axes. The authors call the result a shared organizational cortex.
AI.result: In a registered retrieval experiment, the Dimension term adds 0.028 nDCG@10 (p = 0.002). In system-level comparisons, the full configuration improves nDCG@10 by 0.081 over Signals-only retrieval and by 0.053 over graph-augmented Signals-only retrieval, both reported at p below 0.001.
AI.conclusion: The architecture gives organizations a persistent, revisable basis for shared judgement.

title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
summary: Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. We propose PAYWORTHY which contains 1{,}494 real freelance job postings, sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. We ask 18 models to forecast how likely the agent is to succeed and measure how well each model's forecasts rank the accepted jobs above the rejected ones (AUC, where 0.5 is a random ranking). The answer depends on how the agent is described. Told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs well (AUC 0.66--0.86). Told instead that it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank the same jobs about as well as a random ordering (0.45--0.56). These results hold under judges from four other model families (Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen), and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether frontier LLMs can predict, before any attempt, whether an AI agent will complete a freelance job. The forecasts are informative only when the agent is described by its limitations; when it is described as a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank jobs at about chance.
AI.motivation: Before an AI agent takes a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed, and it was unknown whether LLMs can make this call from the posting alone.
AI.method: The authors build PAYWORTHY from 1,494 real freelance job postings sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting in a single run, an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work, and 18 models forecast success, scored by AUC. The agent is described in two ways, and judges from four other model families are checked.
AI.result: When told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs with AUC 0.66 to 0.86. When told it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models score 0.45 to 0.56, about random. The results hold under judges from Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen, and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters.
AI.conclusion: Forecasts of agent success depend heavily on how the agent is described, so an agent's stated limitations matter for predicting which jobs it can complete.

title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application
comment: 19 pages. Code, data and interactive demo: this https URL (archived at this https URL)
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

AI.tldr: The paper applies FlyHash, a fruit-fly-inspired hashing scheme of sparse random projection with winner-take-all competition, to LLM agent memory retrieval. FlyHash improves neighbor quality per bit over SimHash, but it gives no practical memory or latency savings, and HNSW dominates both hashing methods at ordinary scale.
AI.motivation: LLM agents store memories as dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. Prior work showed FlyHash preserves neighbor structure better per bit than SimHash on several benchmarks, but this had not been tested for agent memory retrieval.
AI.method: The authors apply FlyHash to agent memory retrieval across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, under a matched-bit protocol that corrects a comparison pitfall. They compare against SimHash and HNSW, introduce a sparse-set latency comparison, and test against agent-memory relevance labels that are not circular.
AI.result: The quality advantage holds under matched bits. At equal bits FlyHash codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash codes, and HNSW dominates both hashing methods at ordinary scale. The sparse-set comparison recovers most but not all of the naive latency gap. The quality advantage survives the non-circular relevance labels.
AI.conclusion: The practical case for hashing in agent memory is narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies, and the authors release their implementation, a working demo and an account of the methodological pitfalls they found.

title: Consistency Is Not Understanding: Orbit Audits for Neural Field Weight Readers
summary: Recognizing visual content from neural-network weights requires separating functional information from arbitrary parameter coordinates. We audit this separation with hidden-neuron permutations and positive ReLU rescalings that preserve the represented function. The study contains 480 independently fitted shape fields and 1,000 MNIST fields, with transformed copies grouped by origin. On shape recognition, a statistics reader falls from \ShapeRawStats\% to \ShapeJointStats\% accuracy under joint transformations; a normalized set reader retains \ShapeNormSet\% with unchanged predictions. Four small frozen language models obtain \LMRange\% raw accuracy with next-token scoring. A separate four-configuration reasoning experiment with 1,920 scored sessions obtains \FrontRawRange\% raw accuracy with generated answers, while fresh identical raw prompts disagree on \FrontRawRepeatRange\% of origins. Canonicalization makes equivalent prompts identical, but this neither establishes recognition nor guarantees identical generated responses. Joint correctness/agreement metrics, semantic-cue controls, fresh repeats, and exact-rational rounding bounds separate these failure modes. The result is an inspectable evaluation protocol for visual weight readers, with claims restricted to the tested fields, prompts, and execution configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether visual weight readers, which recognize content from neural-network weights, capture function or merely parameter coordinates, using function-preserving hidden-neuron permutations and positive ReLU rescalings. A statistics-based reader's accuracy falls sharply under joint transformations, while a normalized set reader keeps its accuracy with unchanged predictions.
AI.motivation: Recognizing visual content from network weights requires separating functional information from arbitrary parameter coordinates, and existing evaluations do not test this separation.
AI.method: The study uses 480 independently fitted shape fields and 1,000 MNIST fields, with transformed copies grouped by origin. It evaluates a statistics reader, a normalized set reader, four small frozen language models using next-token scoring, and a reasoning experiment with 1,920 scored sessions. Joint correctness and agreement metrics, semantic-cue controls, fresh repeated prompts and exact-rational rounding bounds separate the failure modes.
AI.result: On shape recognition, the statistics reader's accuracy falls under joint transformations, while the normalized set reader retains its accuracy with unchanged predictions. The four small frozen language models obtain raw accuracies that the paper reports as a range. In the reasoning experiment, fresh identical raw prompts disagree on a reported share of origins, and canonicalization makes equivalent prompts identical without guaranteeing identical generated responses.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers an inspectable evaluation protocol for visual weight readers, with claims restricted to the tested fields, prompts and execution configurations; canonicalization alone establishes neither recognition nor consistent responses.

title: Autonomy and Coordination in Intelligent Manufacturing: A Recursive Autonomous Agent Framework
summary: Intelligent production requires systems to make decisions and organize work according to production goals and operating conditions. It also requires continuous adjustment through feedback. This paper analyzes intelligence in human production organizations from a complex adaptive systems (CAS) perspective. The analysis identifies two coupled mechanisms: individual autonomy and collective coordination. Individual autonomy enables actors to form local decisions using available information. Collective coordination aligns these decisions with shared goals and joint constraints. Learning and adaptation improve both mechanisms over time. A production-system model formalizes how local decision rules and coordination jointly form system decisions. On this basis, we propose the Recursive Autonomous Agent (RAA) framework, which combines goal-driven autonomous agents with a recursive organizational structure. Goal contracts define local objectives and operating boundaries, while capability contracts support the selection and composition of production units. Common interfaces allow coordinated groups to participate as units in larger organizations, connecting equipment, production lines, and factories. RAA thus provides an engineering approach to next-generation intelligent manufacturing, translating the requirements of intelligence, openness, and system-wide integration into mechanisms for autonomous and coordinated production.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Recursive Autonomous Agent (RAA) framework for intelligent manufacturing, combining goal-driven autonomous agents with a recursive organizational structure. The design is grounded in a complex adaptive systems analysis of individual autonomy and collective coordination.
AI.motivation: Intelligent production requires systems that make decisions and organize work according to production goals and operating conditions, and that adjust through feedback. This needs both local autonomy and coordination of decisions with shared goals.
AI.method: The paper analyzes human production organizations from a complex adaptive systems perspective and identifies individual autonomy and collective coordination as coupled mechanisms. It formalizes a production-system model in which local decision rules and coordination jointly form system decisions. RAA uses goal contracts for local objectives and operating boundaries, capability contracts for selecting and composing production units, and common interfaces so that coordinated groups can act as units in larger organizations.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments or quantitative results; it is a conceptual and modeling contribution.
AI.conclusion: RAA is presented as an engineering approach to next-generation intelligent manufacturing that connects equipment, production lines and factories through autonomous and coordinated production.

title: Vision Paper: Why Distributed LLM Post-Training and Decentralized Alignment Are Now Essential
summary: This vision paper argues that distributed learning, including federated and decentralized, should become a first-class paradigm in LLM post-training, not merely a privacy add-on. Current methods like RLHF and DPO rest on an invisible assumption: preference data should be centralized. We contend this assumption is scientifically unjustified, practically unsustainable, and ethically problematic. As LLMs deploy into healthcare, law, finance, and multilingual communities, preference data originates from populations that cannot or will not centralize. We develop a three-pillar argument grounded in (1) privacy and data sovereignty, (2) pluralism and representational equity, and (3) robustness and scalability. We formalize key technical challenges unique to this intersection, reference drift, preference heterogeneity, and the DP-utility trade-off for contrastive losses, and propose concrete algorithmic directions, and sketch a research agenda. Our analysis shows distributed post-training is not only necessary but tractable, and ignoring it risks AI that is legally noncompliant, representationally narrow, and brittle at scale.

AI.tldr: This vision paper argues that federated and decentralized learning should be a first-class paradigm for LLM post-training rather than a privacy add-on, because preference data often cannot be centralized. It frames three pillars and sketches the technical challenges and a research agenda.
AI.motivation: RLHF and DPO assume that preference data is centralized, which the authors contend is scientifically unjustified, practically unsustainable and ethically problematic as LLMs are deployed in healthcare, law, finance and multilingual communities.
AI.method: The authors develop a three-pillar argument based on privacy and data sovereignty, pluralism and representational equity, and robustness and scalability. They formalize challenges including reference drift, preference heterogeneity and the DP-utility trade-off for contrastive losses, propose algorithmic directions and sketch a research agenda.
AI.result: The paper reports no experiments; its analysis argues that distributed post-training is necessary and tractable.
AI.conclusion: Ignoring distributed post-training risks AI that is legally noncompliant, representationally narrow and brittle at scale.

title: Risk Control Certifies Rates, Not Magnitudes: An Audit of Selective Fetal Biometry
summary: Prenatal ultrasound biometry must return a head circumference (HC) and refuse when the image cannot support one. Selective prediction trades coverage against error, but its finite-sample guarantees bound the rate of gross errors, not their magnitude. We audit a tool-grounded biometry pipeline on two separately pre-registered four-way splits of the 999 labelled HC18 images, retraining the segmenter three times on each. Calibrating the contour-completeness threshold by exact Clopper-Pearson risk control returns a certificate indistinguishable from a hand-set floor, yet the pipeline still emits a 271.3 mm error: a small, geometrically complete ring fitted to an image whose true HC is 324.6 mm. The accepted candidate scores 0.94 completeness, so the score cannot see the failure, and one outlier among $\approx 150$ answers leaves the certified risk bound ($\alpha = 0.10$) intact. A second, untouched split reproduces the mechanism on a different image (233.3 mm). Constraining the admissibility region---the anatomical range in which the measurand is defined---removes the family instead: raising the lower bound from 50 to 55 mm costs 0.4 coverage points and cuts the worst-case error on both splits to 11.4 and 11.1 mm, whereas suppressing it through the completeness threshold costs 19.0 and 12.1 points. At an anatomically defined 70 mm the frozen tests give 1.91 and 1.81 mm MAE.

AI.tldr: The paper audits a tool-grounded fetal biometry pipeline and shows that finite-sample risk control certifies the rate of gross errors but not their magnitude: the pipeline emits a 271.3 mm head circumference error while its certified risk bound stays intact. Constraining the admissible anatomical range removes this failure family and yields low error at a defined range.
AI.motivation: Selective prediction gives finite-sample guarantees on the rate of gross errors but not on their size, which matters for prenatal ultrasound head circumference estimates, where the system must either return a value or refuse.
AI.method: The authors audit the pipeline on two separately pre-registered four-way splits of the 999 labelled HC18 images, retraining the segmenter three times on each. They calibrate a contour-completeness threshold by exact Clopper-Pearson risk control and compare the result with a hand-set floor. They also test raising the lower bound of the admissible range from 50 to 55 mm against suppressing errors through the completeness threshold.
AI.result: Risk-control calibration returns a certificate indistinguishable from a hand-set floor, yet one outlier among about 150 answers gives a 271.3 mm error on an image whose true head circumference is 324.6 mm, with a completeness score of 0.94. A second, untouched split reproduces the mechanism on a different image, with a 233.3 mm error. Raising the lower bound to 55 mm costs 0.4 coverage points and cuts the worst-case error to 11.4 and 11.1 mm on the two splits, whereas suppressing through the completeness threshold costs 19.0 and 12.1 points. At an anatomically defined 70 mm, the frozen tests give MAE of 1.91 and 1.81 mm.
AI.conclusion: Risk control certifies rates rather than magnitudes, so the admissible range must be constrained anatomically; the paper argues that certification in medical measurement has to account for error magnitude as well as error rate.

title: Auditable Unlearning for LLMs
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove a user's data from a trained model after a deletion request. Existing methods are majorly evaluated on three axes - how well they forget, how much capability they retain, and how robust they are to membership inference attacks, but not on whether the provider can offer the user any evidence that the deletion occurred. To fill this gap, we introduce auditability as a fourth axis, defined as the separation between requested (forget set) and retained (retain set) data under a statistic the provider computes. We show that across eleven unlearning methods on TOFU, MUSE and RWKU no method satisfies all four axes, with different methods falling short on different axes. To address this, we propose a two stage method that can be used on top of any unlearning method, in the the first stage we propose ${GapWiden}$ which uses a hinge loss to increase the difference between audit statistics of forget set and retain set. In the second stage we propose ${GapVeil}$, an inference time rejection-sampler which uses the base model as the drafter and re-samples based on the audit statistics of the drafted response. We observe that using our method, auditability and leakage reach oracle parity for every unlearning method, and forget performance converges to the oracle; retain performance improves for nine of eleven methods but remains short of parity. Our results show that evidence of deletion or auditability can be constructed by design, and that treating it as an explicit requirement changes the viability of existing unlearning methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces auditability as a fourth axis for LLM unlearning, measuring whether a provider can show evidence that a deletion occurred. None of eleven existing methods satisfies all four axes, and the proposed two-stage method, GapWiden plus GapVeil, reaches oracle parity on auditability and leakage for every method.
AI.motivation: Unlearning is evaluated on forgetting, retained capability and robustness to membership inference, but not on whether the provider can offer evidence that a deletion happened.
AI.method: Auditability is defined as the separation between forget-set and retain-set data under a statistic the provider computes. GapWiden, the first stage, uses a hinge loss to widen the gap between the audit statistics of the forget and retain sets. GapVeil, the second stage, is an inference-time rejection sampler that uses the base model as drafter and resamples based on the audit statistics of the drafted response. The evaluation covers eleven unlearning methods on TOFU, MUSE and RWKU.
AI.result: No method satisfies all four axes, with different methods falling short on different axes. With the proposed method, auditability and leakage reach oracle parity for every unlearning method and forget performance converges to the oracle. Retain performance improves for nine of eleven methods but remains short of parity.
AI.conclusion: Evidence of deletion can be built into unlearning by design, and treating auditability as an explicit requirement changes the viability of existing unlearning methods.

title: RECAP: Context-Aware Prediction Recycling with Request-Local and Persistent Memories for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
summary: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RECAP, a training-free speculative decoding method for vision-language models that recycles the target model's own predictions, indexed by one-, two- and three-token keys, with request-local contextual memories. It reaches mean speedups of 1.66x and 1.56x over autoregressive decoding on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, above the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling.
AI.motivation: Existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, which conflates predictions computed under different images and prefixes, so reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states.
AI.method: RECAP stores target predictions under one-, two- and three-token keys. Contextual memories live only for the current request and are therefore implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests. Entropy-confidence weighting fuses retrieved predictions by key specificity and concentration, best-first search composes them into a candidate tree supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding.
AI.result: Across seven single-turn benchmarks, mean speedups over autoregressive decoding are 1.66x on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 1.56x on LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding Token Recycling at 1.51x and 1.37x. No training or auxiliary draft model is needed.
AI.conclusion: Image-aware, multi-length prediction recycling gives a training-free route to faster VLM decoding and outperforms the strongest prior training-free baseline.

title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback
summary: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EchoKV, a KV cache eviction method that corrects early workspace errors through iterative query feedback. On LongBench it improves over LAQ on tasks that require dispersed evidence, such as multi-hop cross-document QA, while keeping comparable performance on the remaining subsets.
AI.motivation: KV cache eviction depends on the workspace used to generate eviction queries, so an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce a wrong eviction decision, especially when evidence is dispersed across a long context.
AI.method: EchoKV initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace from proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ and adds a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair.
AI.result: On LongBench's 16 tasks with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several dispersed-evidence tasks, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension, and comparable performance on the remaining subsets across budgets and backbones.
AI.conclusion: Query-workspace coupling is identified as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction, and iterative correction addresses it.

title: CHARM+: Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism
summary: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.

AI.tldr: CHARM+ is a sequence-parallel attention method for LLMs that reorganizes Ring-Attention communication into levels and decouples cross-hardware from intra-hardware traffic to improve GPU utilization. Against Ring-Attention it reports average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x (forward and backward) on a dual-NUMA PCIe system and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink system.
AI.motivation: Ring-Attention style sequence parallelism is the mainstream way to handle long sequences, but its communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, and imbalanced bandwidth in NUMA or multi-node architectures makes frequent synchronization limit overall performance.
AI.method: CHARM+ (Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism) reorganizes sequential communications into several levels to obtain intra-level parallelism and computation overlap, and decouples cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication to eliminate the synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance.
AI.result: The forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods; compared with Ring-Attention they achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware reorganization of attention communication can recover the GPU utilization lost to communication dependencies and bandwidth imbalance in long-sequence LLM attention.

title: Autonomous agents for electricity-system planning
summary: Planning electricity systems requires repeated decisions that connect regional resources, investment, operation and network constraints. Here we present an autonomous planning framework that carries prepared regional scenarios through proposal, numerical evaluation, feedback interpretation, redesign and final plan selection. Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions and feeder interventions, interpret numerical feedback, and decide how to revise designs and when to stop. The framework automatically executes annual investment-and-dispatch optimization and representative-feeder verification, applies fixed acceptance criteria and retains the lowest-cost accepted candidate. We evaluate forty carbon-constrained trajectories across ten system-year scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries, using two model deployments and single- and multi-agent architectures. All forty retain candidates satisfying the implemented physical and fixed annual operational carbon-budget checks. Twenty-eight of forty matched reference designs exceed the new scenario ceilings. A separate archive of ninety-six trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual ceiling provides matched references and broader regional coverage. The results demonstrate autonomous planning under explicit emissions constraints using public regional data and published institutional demand outlooks.

AI.tldr: An autonomous agent framework for electricity-system planning carries regional scenarios through proposal, numerical evaluation, feedback interpretation, redesign and final plan selection. All forty tested carbon-constrained trajectories retained candidates that pass the implemented physical and annual carbon-budget checks.
AI.motivation: Electricity-system planning requires repeated decisions that connect regional resources, investment, operation and network constraints, and iterating on these decisions by hand under explicit emissions limits is laborious.
AI.method: Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions and feeder interventions, interpret numerical feedback, and decide how to revise designs and when to stop; the framework automatically runs annual investment-and-dispatch optimization and representative-feeder verification, applies fixed acceptance criteria, and retains the lowest-cost accepted candidate.
AI.result: Forty carbon-constrained trajectories across ten system-year scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries were evaluated with two model deployments and single- and multi-agent architectures; all forty retained candidates satisfying the implemented physical and fixed annual carbon-budget checks, and 28 of the 40 matched reference designs exceed the new scenario ceilings. A separate archive of 96 trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual ceiling supplies matched references and broader regional coverage.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate autonomous planning under explicit emissions constraints, using public regional data and published institutional demand outlooks.

title: Routes of Reasoning: Reading and Reshaping Test-Time Compute in MoE Models
summary: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the router logits of Mixture-of-Experts reasoning models can label the reasoning behavior of each token and can be edited at inference to curb overthinking. The edit reduces generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (up to 63.3%) across four models and four benchmarks, and accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models often keep verifying and re-deriving long after finding a correct answer, which wastes test-time compute, and existing interventions such as token budgets or steering regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors.
AI.method: Reasoning traces are split into sentence-level segments, each labelled with one of six behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, conclusion); linear probes on MoE router logits predict these labels nearly as well as residual-stream probes while using about half as many features, and experts associated with a behavior transfer across six datasets. Selectively editing expert router scores during inference then curbs overthinking without training.
AI.result: Across four models and four benchmarks the intervention reduces generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (up to 63.3%), accuracy drops by no more than 0.5 percentage points and frequently improves, and the model stops once the problem is solved instead of skipping essential reasoning steps.
AI.conclusion: MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight, training-free mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.

title: Split-KV: Efficient Context Parallelism for Training Diffusion Drafters
summary: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Split-KV is an exact context-parallelism method for training diffusion drafters that keeps key/value shards local and communicates only query-sized tensors. At CP size 64 it retains 85-91% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to 3.67x speedup over the fastest available CP baseline.
AI.motivation: Diffusion drafters with anchor sampling cross-attend short draft queries to a much longer context, but no existing context-parallelism method exploits this query-context asymmetry while meeting the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement that anchor sampling creates.
AI.method: Split-KV keeps key/value shards local so that per-layer attention communication is limited to query-sized tensors and does not depend on context length; its global query view enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost.
AI.result: At CP size 64, Split-KV retains 85-91% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to 3.67x speedup over the fastest available CP baseline; LPT achieves less than 1% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the query-context asymmetry makes context parallelism for training diffusion drafters both efficient and scalable.

title: Graph-Mediated Large Language Model Systems in the Agentic Era: Reasoning, Knowledge, Retrieval, Execution, and Coordination
summary: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.

AI.tldr: This survey organizes graph operations in LLM systems by their role and the component that computes them, covering reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. It also turns these into an evaluation framework and lists open challenges.
AI.motivation: Graphs now support structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, memory, execution dependencies and multi-agent communication in LLM systems, but it is unclear what each graph operation contributes, which component computes it, and how its output is subsequently used.
AI.method: The survey introduces an operation-level role-locus taxonomy and compares how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery.
AI.result: The comparisons separate improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance and keep the conditions under which results were reported; benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics and system costs are organized into an evaluation framework.
AI.conclusion: The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages, and it identifies open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery.

title: From Waste to Discovery: Recycling High-Scored Unexposed Candidates in Taobao Feed Recommendation
summary: Helping users discover new interests is vital to the long-term health of industrial recommender systems, yet the usual remedy, boosting exposure of under-explored (discovery) content, often backfires in production. We report URED (Unexposed Recycling for Efficient Discovery), a training-free recall-stage system serving Taobao feed recommendation at Alibaba for over six months to tens of millions of daily active users. It rests on a production-validated insight: naive boosting fails because it injects cold, information-poor candidates that rankers systematically over-estimate, buying no discovery gain while risking engagement. Items scored highly but never exposed (signals industrial pipelines routinely discard) form a pool that is both relevant and reliably predictable. Over a 30-day horizon URED aggregates them and re-injects at recall time through a lightweight pipeline spanning offline storage, distributed aggregation, and low-latency online serving, adding under 1% latency via a single O(1) lookup per request with no model retraining. Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved: completion video views rise significantly (+2.62%) and total views move positive (+0.36%, not significant). Ablations confirm both design pillars are necessary: a one-day window collapses the discovery gain to +0.55% (not significant), and random injection without score filtering yields no gain while trending negative on engagement (-0.17%). Across production recall channels, URED reaches 13.9x the platform-average discovery rate (6.3x the strongest nearline baseline) at engagement quality on par with the platform average. We share deployment details and lessons for practitioners facing the exploration-exploitation dilemma under tight resource constraints.

AI.tldr: URED is a training-free recall-stage system serving Taobao feed recommendation that recycles items scored highly by the ranker but never exposed, and re-injects them at recall time. Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved.
AI.motivation: Boosting exposure of under-explored discovery content often backfires in production because it injects cold, information-poor candidates that rankers systematically over-estimate, which yields no discovery gain and risks engagement.
AI.method: Items scored highly but never exposed, a pool that industrial pipelines routinely discard, are aggregated over a 30-day horizon and re-injected at recall time through offline storage, distributed aggregation and low-latency online serving, with a single O(1) lookup per request and no model retraining.
AI.result: Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness, with completion video views rising significantly (+2.62%) and total views moving positive (+0.36%, not significant). A one-day window collapses the discovery gain to +0.55% (not significant), and random injection without score filtering yields no gain while engagement trends negative (-0.17%). Across recall channels URED reaches 13.9x the platform-average discovery rate and 6.3x the strongest nearline baseline, at engagement quality on par with the platform average.
AI.conclusion: Recycling unexposed high-scored candidates offers a practical way to address the exploration-exploitation dilemma under tight resource constraints, and the paper shares deployment details and lessons for practitioners.

title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables. Website: this https URL
summary: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.

AI.tldr: Reglos is a training-free personal memory agent whose harness improves through recursive self-improvement, with a critic from a second model family screening each patch for benchmark gaming and a fixed evaluator deciding which patches to accept. With the same backbone it outperforms Mem0, MemOS and EverOS on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S.
AI.motivation: Coding agents now rewrite the harness that turns each user's memory into model context, but a patch tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else, so such patches risk overfitting.
AI.method: Each user's append-only memory is updated with every conversation, with new preferences superseding old ones and facts able to be forgotten; a coding agent proposes harness patches from failure traces, a critic from a second model family screens each patch for benchmark gaming, and after the harness is frozen a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept.
AI.result: With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos reaches 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna, outperforming state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS.
AI.conclusion: Testing whether harness changes help beyond their target failures is presented as a way to keep self-improving personal memory agents from overfitting.

title: Which One Is Sounding? Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation
summary: Existing audio-visual segmentation methods mainly predict sound-related regions or category masks and often fail to identify the sounding instance when multiple same-class candidates coexist. Recent audio-visual instance segmentation methods address instance-level prediction but rely largely on motion and cross-frame association, which may become unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion. To this end, we introduce binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source-direction information, to provide spatial constraints for distinguishing the sounding instance among same-class visual candidates. We propose Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation (BiSID-AVS), which progressively refines category-level candidate responses into a mask of the true sounding instance. BiSID-AVS first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels. Experiments on the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception show that BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on the multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points, respectively, while substantially reducing false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.

AI.tldr: BiSID-AVS uses the interaural differences in binaural audio to identify which of several same-class visual candidates is the true sounding instance in audio-visual segmentation. It improves instance-level mIoU on multi-candidate subsets by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Audio-visual segmentation methods predict sound-related regions or category masks and fail to identify the sounding instance when same-class candidates coexist, while instance-level methods rely on motion and cross-frame association, which becomes unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion.
AI.method: Binaural audio supplies spatial constraints; the model first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels.
AI.result: On the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and the Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception, BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points respectively, and substantially reduces false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.
AI.conclusion: Binaural spatial cues can disambiguate the sounding instance among same-class candidates where motion-based association is unreliable.

title: UniCompress: From Multi-LoRA Experts to One Compact Model for Edge Intelligence
summary: Embodied and edge systems increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to support heterogeneous skills, yet deploying a separate task adapter for each skill while retaining a high-precision backbone creates substantial memory and management costs. We present UniCompress, a deployment-oriented framework that converts multi-task expertise into one compact, adapter-free model. Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, UniCompress constructs an asymmetric INT2 student using GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. The approach jointly quantizes and recovers the projection weights in the vision encoder and language backbone, enabling aggressive compression of the complete vision-language model while preserving its multi-task behavior. We evaluate UniCompress on four heterogeneous embodied tasks: posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction. UniCompress reduces the approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB in INT2, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 76%. It improves the INT2 macro task score by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 while remaining within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher. These results demonstrate the potential of teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery for deploying a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.

AI.tldr: UniCompress converts a multi-task vision-language model into one adapter-free INT2 model through teacher-guided quantization recovery. It cuts approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB, a reduction of about 76%, while staying within 0.9 points of the BF16 teacher.
AI.motivation: Embodied and edge systems that deploy a separate task adapter for each skill while keeping a high-precision backbone incur substantial memory and management costs.
AI.method: Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, an asymmetric INT2 student is built with GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery, jointly quantizing and recovering the projection weights in both the vision encoder and the language backbone.
AI.result: Across four heterogeneous embodied tasks (posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing and mobile-GUI action prediction), the INT2 macro task score improves by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 and remains within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery shows the potential to deploy a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.

title: Reasoning-Trace Overflow in Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Explicit Reasoning Models
summary: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of relatively small open-weight reasoning models across six code benchmark settings finds that reasoning can consume a fixed 32k-token output budget before any usable code is produced. Disabling reasoning can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while budgeted transitions give more direct control.
AI.motivation: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it can also consume so much of the output budget that the model never produces usable code, a risk the paper frames as reasoning-trace overflow.
AI.method: Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, the authors measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls (prompt steering and budgeted transitions) mitigate overflow.
AI.result: Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks but common on harder code benchmarks and for particular model families; on several model-benchmark pairs more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k budget. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Prompt steering substantially reduces overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions give more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models.
AI.conclusion: Explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation rather than an always-on capability, since its value is conditional on model strength and task difficulty.

title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
summary: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MechScam is a 6,614-video benchmark that explains scam mechanisms with video evidence and includes misleading arguments, and ScamCourt is a debate framework whose judge decides from verified citations. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives.
AI.motivation: Existing scam video studies are mostly binary classifiers that give limited insight into how scams work, and they overlook the difficulty of separating scams from superficially similar non-scam content such as advertisements and the robustness of detectors to misleading arguments.
AI.method: MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence; ScamCourt stages trained prosecution and defense debaters who present opposing arguments while a trained judge decides from a transcript with verified citations.
AI.result: State-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reduces false positives, and shows stronger resistance to misleading arguments.
AI.conclusion: Together MechScam and ScamCourt aim at more reliable and interpretable scam video detection.

title: From Handcrafted to Generative: RLVR-Optimized Icon Generation for Alexa+
summary: Alexa+ devices with screens display animated icons during conversations to visually reinforce what is being said. The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.

AI.tldr: A deployed pipeline generates vectorised animated icons for Alexa+ screens from a text description, and RLVR fine-tuning of its image generation stage raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x). Both the fine-tuned model and the verifier are in production.
AI.motivation: Hand-drawn animated icons cannot scale to the range of topics in open-ended conversation, and supervised fine-tuning is not viable because no dataset of line-art icons exists under the strict small-canvas design constraints.
AI.method: Objective verifiers automatically flag generations that violate the design guidelines, and a flow matching image generation model is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR); the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.
AI.result: The pass rate rises from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-based RLVR can improve the first, quality-determining stage of a production icon pipeline where supervised data is unavailable.

title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
summary: Static and incomplete parametric knowledge limits the performance of multimodal large language models on novel-knowledge and knowledge-intensive tasks, especially those requiring multi-hop evidence acquisition. Existing multimodal agentic search methods often fix visual evidence at the input or a predefined trajectory position, making it difficult for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve and to handle complex real-world queries. We define this capability as autonomous cross-modal search: an agent chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search, and reverse-image search, actively introduces visual evidence when appropriate, and switches between and integrates modalities across multiple hops. We propose ModalSearch-Pipeline, a scalable procedure for constructing an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph. It samples paths with diverse depths and modality compositions and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets that would expose reasoning shortcuts while retaining necessary disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized, and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems. We train the ModalSearcher Agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and construct ModalSearch-Bench. Experiments show that ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ModalSearcher is an agent that autonomously chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search and reverse-image search, and improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks. It is trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal agentic search methods fix visual evidence at the input or at a predefined trajectory position, which makes it hard for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve across multi-hop, complex queries.
AI.method: ModalSearch-Pipeline builds an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph by sampling paths of diverse depths and modality compositions, and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets while keeping the disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems; the ModalSearcher agent is trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment.
AI.result: ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks; the authors also construct ModalSearch-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous cross-modal search, in which visual evidence is introduced when appropriate and modalities are switched and integrated across hops, is a useful capability for knowledge-intensive multimodal QA.

title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models.
