We further formalize certification under sequences of repeated deletion requests, where cross-shard distillation can create dependencies between shards; we prove that a closure-based cascading retraining procedure restores the deletion guarantee to the full aggregated model under any deletion sequence. Experiments on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, BiLSTM/IMDB, TCN/IMDB, and a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST show $14-91\%$ better selective forgetting, up to $50\%$ better utility retention in relative terms (with consistent percentage-point gains on the other architectures, where a relative baseline is undefined), and unlearning-time changes ranging from $-6.7\%$ to $+6.4\%$ depending on architecture, relative to SISA.

AI.tldr: IDSISA improves SISA-based certified unlearning by using influence functions to concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards and distillation to recover utility, while keeping an exact deletion guarantee and proving a cascading retraining procedure for repeated deletions.
AI.motivation: Full retraining is prohibitive at scale and approximate unlearning lacks formal guarantees; SISA certifies deletion, but random partitioning scatters forget requests across shards and isolated retraining degrades utility.
AI.method: Influence functions concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards, and distillation from unaffected shards recovers the utility lost to isolation; a closure-based cascading retraining procedure handles sequences of repeated deletion requests, where cross-shard distillation creates dependencies between shards.
AI.result: Across ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, BiLSTM and TCN on IMDB, and a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST, selective forgetting is 14 to 91 percent better and utility retention is up to 50 percent better in relative terms (with percentage-point gains where a relative baseline is undefined), and unlearning time changes from -6.7 to +6.4 percent relative to SISA; the distillation approximation has a certification error at most 0.015 in expectation.
AI.conclusion: The deletion guarantee inherited from SISA's retraining step stays exact and the cascading procedure restores it for the full aggregated model under any deletion sequence, while the utility recovery is a separately quantified, empirically bounded approximation.

title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust)
summary: Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that signals observable before an offspring reproduces can point in opposite directions for entering and for persisting in a Quality-Diversity archive, and biasing parent selection toward them does not improve search.
AI.motivation: Uniform parent sampling in unstructured Quality-Diversity archives gives no way to direct search toward individuals likely to make durable archive contributions, which matters because automated failure discovery is a diversity problem.
AI.method: The authors test whether pre-reproduction signals separate offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later, across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, and then bias parent selection toward the signals most associated with survival.
AI.result: The same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions; lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover; moderate bias matches uniform sampling and strong bias reduces QD-score.
AI.conclusion: A signal's association with survival does not translate into better search when used for parent selection, so such credit assignment is not a simple remedy for failure discovery.

title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains
summary: AI agents rely on third-party tools, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, whose publishers can be authenticated and whose execution can be restricted by runtime security policies. Yet authenticity does not guarantee benign behaviour: a legitimately signed tool may perform its advertised function while concealing malicious code that leaks confidential information. We demonstrate this trust failure with a signed MCP tool that embeds sensitive data in requests to a policy-allowed destination. Meta's MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run, yet fails to prevent this attack in every trial. We introduce germline execution, which limits information disclosure without inspecting or trusting tool implementations. Each tool invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, each receiving only information authorised for its destination. Even if malicious code executes, what it can disclose is bounded by the data available to its copy. Under explicit assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline, we prove sink noninterference for every signed release and, for releases deterministic within our replay model, show that a verified witness establishes a flow violation. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defences and an ablation. Invocations served by a single copy completed in 10-49 ms, 2-28x faster than restarting the tool for every invocation, the conventional way to clear state. These results show that data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a signed MCP tool can leak confidential data while passing authentication, and proposes germline execution, which runs each invocation in an ephemeral copy forked from a data-free germline process so that disclosure is bounded by that copy's data.
AI.motivation: Authenticity of a third-party tool does not guarantee benign behaviour, and MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt yet fails to stop the signed-tool attack in every trial.
AI.method: Each invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, and each copy receives only the information authorised for its destination, so the tool implementation need not be inspected or trusted; sink noninterference is proven under assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline.
AI.result: Across 153 attack runs no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9 to 74.5 percent of runs under baseline defences and an ablation; invocations served by a single copy complete in 10 to 49 ms, which is 2 to 28 times faster than restarting the tool for every invocation.
AI.conclusion: Data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software, under the stated assumptions on copy confinement and the data-free germline.

title: From Reconstruction to Imputation: Test-Time Optimization for Missing Time-Series Channels
summary: Complete sensor-channel failures create a difficult form of time-series missingness: local interpolation is unavailable, and deploying a separately trained imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical. We ask whether a sequence reconstructor trained without artificial mask augmentation and then frozen can be converted into an imputer at inference time. Our method treats the missing entries of each test window as optimization variables, clamps all observations, and backpropagates through the frozen model to minimize reconstruction error only on observed coordinates. The resulting observed-self-consistency objective requires neither artificial mask augmentation nor full-channel dropout during reconstructor training. We characterize when this refinement is informative through the cross-Jacobian from missing inputs to observed residuals, and use an optional temporal-smoothness prior when that coupling is weak. Across five real-world datasets with exactly one channel synthetically masked per test window and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior test-time refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations. Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a frozen sequence reconstructor trained without mask augmentation can be turned into an imputer for missing time-series channels by optimizing the missing entries at test time to minimize reconstruction error on the observed coordinates.
AI.motivation: Complete sensor-channel failures leave no local interpolation to fall back on, and training a separate imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical.
AI.method: The missing entries of each test window are treated as optimization variables, all observations are clamped, and the error is backpropagated through the frozen model on observed coordinates only; an optional temporal-smoothness prior is used when cross-channel coupling is weak, and the cross-Jacobian indicates when refinement is informative.
AI.result: With one channel masked per test window across five datasets and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations; the best refined reconstructor has the lowest MAE on two datasets against mask-aware imputers and trails the strongest baseline on three, and the gains need substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling.
AI.conclusion: Test-time self-consistency is a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.

title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
summary: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.

AI.tldr: Using the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a few large US tech firms early access to a vulnerability-finding model, the paper finds that treated firms disclosed far more high-impact flaws and fixed them as quickly as before, with no evidence that attackers exploited the extra vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws, and it is unclear how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers and attackers.
AI.method: Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, the study compares firms with access to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, and tracks the reports of external bug-bounty researchers and the exploitation of disclosed flaws.
AI.result: Firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to the comparison firms and disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, while fixing reported flaws as quickly as before; external researchers reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code; the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because fewer were already exploited at disclosure, while the number exploited did not change.
AI.conclusion: Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers could exploit them, but the restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.

title: Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget
summary: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that residual hardware noise acts as a regularizer when quantum circuit Born machines are trained with maximum mean discrepancy, and proposes GENIE, which selects the noise level during training from held-out data with bounded regret.
AI.motivation: The value of quantum circuit Born machines depends on generalizing from finite training data, and how hardware noise affects that generalization was unknown.
AI.method: The generalization gap under maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach; scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so the noise strength has an intermediate optimum; GENIE realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget.
AI.result: In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.
AI.conclusion: Noise can be used as a tunable regularizer, and adaptive selection with provably bounded regret beats any fixed noise level.

title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images
summary: We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.

AI.tldr: Trick-or-Treat is an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs, and it shows that frontier models hallucinate photograph findings far more often when the two modalities conflict.
AI.motivation: Existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs, which makes cross-modal medical reasoning hard to evaluate.
AI.method: For each condition, two image pairs share one chest radiograph but contain different synthetic photographs; matched pairs show findings that point to the same diagnosis, mismatched pairs show an alternative finding, and synthetic generation keeps the person and photographic setting constant to reduce confounding.
AI.result: Three frontier models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45 to 57.5 percent of mismatched pairs, up from 25 to 37.5 percent for the same photographs shown alone; when faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore the mismatch and hallucinate findings that matched the radiograph.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes a concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.

title: Human Motion Prediction via Continual Prior Compensation
summary: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) aims to predict future human poses at different moments according to observed past motion sequences. Previous approaches mainly treated the prediction of different temporal moments as a single prediction task and learned the predictions of varied moments simultaneously, which would encounter a main limitation: the learning of short-term predictions (referring to ``near-future'' prediction) could be hindered by the predictions of long-term (referring to ``far-future'' prediction) motions. In this paper, we develop a novel temporal continual learning framework called Continual Prior Compensation (CPC) to progressively train HMP models, in which we divide the prediction task of motions corresponding to varied temporal moments into several subtasks and train the model in a multi-stage manner. To mitigate the prior information forgetting in the progressive training, we further introduce a learnable random variable Prior Compensation Factor (PCF) to explicitly measure the prior knowledge loss. We theoretically show that the PCF can be efficiently learned together with the model parameters by minimizing a reasonable upper bound of the objective function. The proposed CPC is further enhanced to estimate the prior information loss for each subtask and a new framework called Continual Prior Compensation++ (CPC++) with Fine-Grained Prior Compensation Factor (FGPCF) is finally developed. Our CPC and CPC++ frameworks are quite flexible and can be easily integrated with different HMP backbone models and adapted to various datasets and applications. Extensive experiments on three HMP benchmark datasets using multiple SOTA HMP backbones (PGBIG, siMLPe, MotionMixer, and LTD) demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our frameworks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Continual Prior Compensation, which trains human motion prediction in stages over subtasks split by prediction horizon and uses a learnable Prior Compensation Factor to counter forgetting, with CPC++ refining this factor per subtask.
AI.motivation: Learning all prediction horizons jointly lets long-term predictions hinder the learning of short-term ones in human motion prediction models.
AI.method: CPC divides the prediction of different temporal moments into subtasks trained progressively, and a learnable Prior Compensation Factor measures the loss of prior knowledge and is learned by minimizing an upper bound of the objective; CPC++ adds a Fine-Grained Prior Compensation Factor that estimates the prior information loss for each subtask.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three human motion prediction benchmarks with several state-of-the-art backbones (PGBIG, siMLPe, MotionMixer and LTD) demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the frameworks; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The frameworks are flexible, can be integrated with different backbones and adapted to various datasets and applications.

title: AgentTrustCI: Build-Time Policy, Grounding, and Trajectory Tests for Java LLM Agents
comment: Accepted for publication in the 2026 International Conference on Computer and Applications (ICCA)
summary: Infrastructure security does not establish whether an LLM agent selected an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow. AgentTrustCI is a Java/JUnit 5 framework that expresses these application-layer expectations as policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded traces. A deterministic replay implementation supports repeatable build-time tests; a judge interface provides an extension point for optional semantic evaluation. On 55 synthetic cases spanning seven enterprise domains, the full pipeline correctly classifies all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls, including ten non-trivial controls, and misses none of 12 designated critical cases. Each single-layer configuration correctly classifies 35 cases because the corpus deliberately isolates ten faults per layer. A grounded answer obtained through a disallowed sequence illustrates the additional coverage of trajectory checks. Repeated measurements quantify validator execution separately from process startup and reporting. These results establish coverage of the authored regression suite, not production accuracy. We describe a production-trace validation protocol, optional LLM-judge integration, and maintenance of expectations as workflows evolve. The contribution is a practical pattern for expressing behavioral contracts within an existing Java release pipeline.

AI.tldr: AgentTrustCI is a Java/JUnit 5 framework that turns policy, grounding and trajectory expectations for LLM agents into build-time tests over recorded traces.
AI.motivation: Infrastructure security does not establish whether an LLM agent selected an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow.
AI.method: Policy, grounding and trajectory checks run over recorded traces, with a deterministic replay implementation for repeatable build-time tests and a judge interface as an extension point for optional semantic evaluation.
AI.result: On 55 synthetic cases across seven enterprise domains, the full pipeline correctly classifies all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls, including ten non-trivial controls, and misses none of 12 designated critical cases; each single-layer configuration classifies 35 cases correctly; the authors state these results establish coverage of the authored regression suite, not production accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a practical pattern for expressing behavioral contracts within an existing Java release pipeline, and production-trace validation is described as a protocol rather than shown.

title: Don't Replace, Complement: A Detector-Agnostic Subspace Signal for Near-OOD Detection
summary: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is mature on far-OOD yet remains weak on near-OOD. These two settings differ in their use of class-characteristic feature directions: far-OOD inputs largely fail to activate those of their predicted class, whereas near-OOD inputs activate them much as in-distribution samples do. Because the axis separating far-OOD leaves near-OOD almost indistinguishable from ID, a score optimized for one setting is misaligned with the other; where a detector already saturates far-OOD, added near-OOD sensitivity is bought partly against it. This divergence motivates a targeted near-OOD signal designed to complement existing scores. We propose PLUS (Per-class Low-dimensional sUbspace Signal). For each class, PLUS selects the $m$ most class-active neurons from a sparse autoencoder, orthonormalizes the corresponding decoder directions to form a low-dimensional subspace, and scores an input by its per-class whitened squared Mahalanobis distance $z$ within the subspace of its predicted class. Designed as a dedicated complement rather than a standalone detector, the signal $z$ is fused additively with any calibrated base score at a single, fixed weight. This weight is a single global constant: no value is adjusted per backbone, per OOD dataset, or per deployment, and all calibration statistics are estimated from ID validation data alone. When applied to 18 existing detectors spanning diverse method families, $z$ consistently improves near-OOD AUROC in all 126 detector--backbone combinations. Far-OOD performance is broadly maintained or improved, with only marginal declines where the base score is near-optimal, making $z$ a robust, detector-agnostic complement across backbones.

AI.tldr: PLUS is a detector-agnostic per-class subspace signal built from sparse autoencoder features that complements existing post-hoc detectors and consistently improves near-OOD AUROC across 126 detector-backbone combinations.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc OOD detection is mature for far-OOD but weak for near-OOD, where inputs activate their class-characteristic directions much as in-distribution samples do, so a score optimized for far-OOD is misaligned with near-OOD.
AI.method: For each class, PLUS selects the m most class-active neurons from a sparse autoencoder, orthonormalizes their decoder directions into a low-dimensional subspace, and scores an input by its per-class whitened squared Mahalanobis distance within the subspace of its predicted class; this score is fused additively with any calibrated base score at one fixed global weight, with calibration statistics estimated from in-distribution validation data alone.
AI.result: Applied to 18 existing detectors spanning diverse method families, the signal improves near-OOD AUROC in all 126 detector-backbone combinations, and far-OOD performance is broadly maintained or improved, with marginal declines only where the base score is near-optimal.
AI.conclusion: The signal is a robust, detector-agnostic complement across backbones, and its single global weight needs no tuning per backbone, OOD dataset or deployment.

title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
comment: 8 pages main body, 10 pages appendix, 1 figure
summary: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

AI.tldr: ALTO is a crowdsourced and actively annotated dataset of 3022 instances of tech-facilitated gender-based violence in Levantine Arabic, African French and Swahili, and existing harmful-content detectors miss many of these instances, especially covert harms.
AI.motivation: Gendered harm detection is dominated by data and models from Global North languages, leaving tech-facilitated gender-based violence in these regional languages under-resourced.
AI.method: Working with civil society organizations in Jordan, Francophone West Africa and Kenya, the authors crowdsourced culturally and linguistically relevant instances and annotated them with active learning to build a small but performant dataset.
AI.result: Existing harmful content detection models show poor recall on ALTO and improve with fine-tuning; models often miss covert harms across all three languages, and error rates are markedly higher in Swahili.
AI.conclusion: The authors release the annotation taxonomy, the dataset and the trained models to support better detection of tech-facilitated gender-based violence in these languages.

title: Beyond the principle-practice gap: Responsible AI as situated epistemic and ethical practice
summary: Responsible AI scholarship has found that ethical principles are frequently not reflected in AI design and development. Conceptualised as a `gap' between principle and practice, this is framed as a problem of implementation, awareness or compliance, and by implication, a deficit of systems or individual behaviour. This paper sets out an alternative explanation. Drawing on fourteen semi-structured interviews with actors designing and governing AI-enabled anti-trafficking systems across law enforcement, commercial, research, and survivor-support contexts, it argues that such apparent gaps emerge from the varied and complex institutional and professional conditions through which actors come to recognise some issues, but not others, as ethical problems requiring action. We show that epistemic choices are intertwined with ethical judgements, and trace four interconnected moments---perception, judgement, situated action and socio-technical materialisation---through which concerns become intelligible, are weighed and acted upon, and are embedded in technical artefacts and governance arrangements. Actors often hold genuine ethical commitments, but these commitments are shaped by institutional logics and professional moral economies: some concerns are materialised, while others are narrowed, deferred or left unrealised. We show that ethical agency is exercised within and between competing constraints of profession, role, prior experience, and institutional settings. The paper argues that responsible AI governance requires purposeful and well-developed epistemic infrastructures that can cut across these constraints to establish institutional conditions through which the knowledge of affected communities and potential harms becomes receivable and actionable in design.

AI.tldr: Drawing on fourteen semi-structured interviews with actors designing and governing AI-enabled anti-trafficking systems, the paper argues that the principle-practice gap in responsible AI reflects institutional and professional conditions shaping what counts as an ethical problem, not simply deficient implementation.
AI.motivation: Responsible AI scholarship frames the gap between ethical principles and AI design as a problem of implementation, awareness or compliance, and the paper contests this framing.
AI.method: Fourteen interviews across law enforcement, commercial, research and survivor-support contexts are analysed through four interconnected moments (perception, judgement, situated action and socio-technical materialisation) by which concerns become intelligible, are weighed and are embedded in technical artefacts and governance.
AI.result: Actors often hold genuine ethical commitments, but these are shaped by institutional logics and professional moral economies, so some concerns are materialised while others are narrowed, deferred or left unrealised; ethical agency is exercised within competing constraints of profession, role, prior experience and institutional setting.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI governance requires epistemic infrastructures that let the knowledge of affected communities and potential harms become receivable and actionable in design.

title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Rel-Bloom, a multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions that tests whether language models reason over facts supplied in the prompt across Bloom-inspired levels and veracity conditions. Accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, and Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for near-ceiling models.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation assumes models reason over relations stated in their context rather than relying on associations memorized during pretraining, but this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning has not been studied in isolation.
AI.method: Builds 450 questions from 30 Wikidata relations, each instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized), with facts supplied directly in the prompt; evaluates 43 models across six languages and two multilingual settings.
AI.result: Across 226,800 predictions, accuracy falls sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, by up to 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Gemini 3.1 Pro averages 99.5% on the other four levels but 60.7% on Evaluate. Item and relation difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, and removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes.
AI.conclusion: Greater model capability does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence.

title: Dexterous Robotic Hands in the Foundation-Model Era: A Full-Stack Survey of Hardware, Data, Cross-Embodiment Transfer, Learning, and Evaluation
comment: 45 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables. Structured narrative review of hardware, data, cross-embodiment transfer, foundation models, tactile sensing, and evaluation for dexterous robotic hands
summary: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.

AI.tldr: A structured narrative survey of dexterous robotic hands in the foundation-model era, organized into five layers (hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; evaluation and applications) and covering work up to early November 2026. It identifies eleven open problems and proposes reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons for more measurable progress.
AI.motivation: Progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation for dexterous hands is usually assessed separately, even though these hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models.
AI.method: Organizes the literature into five interdependent layers, with human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing as cross-cutting perspectives, connected by a system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses; separates within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results.
AI.result: The review is a narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization.
AI.conclusion: The value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment rather than recording volume alone, shared action representations do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact, and task completion alone does not establish physical correctness or deployment readiness.

title: Smartphone-Aided VR Exergames for HIIT: Gamifying Fitness with Real-Time Pose Estimation
summary: This paper introduces an innovative virtual reality (VR) exergame system designed to gamify High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workouts through 11 predefined combo moves, including squat-punch combinations, bilateral arm strikes, and diagonal stretch combos. Unlike conventional tracking methods that often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset-based sensors, our system uses a standard smartphone camera placed on a tripod to capture full-body movement. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative, particularly well-suited to the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT routines. The smartphone footage is processed in real time using a pose estimation algorithm, with extracted biomechanical data analyzed by a backend server built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to structured data sources and tools, and a GPT-4o large language model. The system generates personalized assessments of form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity, and potential injury risks, tailored specifically to high-impact, time-sensitive exercises. A within-subject study involving 20 participants (ages 18-25) compared experiences in VR and Non-VR HIIT sessions. Results indicated significantly higher enjoyment (Mean = 3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), improved immersion/focus (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03), and increased likelihood to recommend (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04) under the VR condition. Confidence to continue did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.15), while perceived intensity remained comparable. The MCP system showed strong agreement with expert evaluation (87.5%, N = 10 sessions, one certified trainer), supporting its reliability as a feedback tool.

AI.tldr: Presents a VR exergame that gamifies HIIT through 11 combo moves, using a smartphone camera with real-time pose estimation and a backend built on the Model Context Protocol and GPT-4o for personalized feedback. In a 20-participant within-subject study, the VR condition raised enjoyment, immersion and likelihood to recommend, and the system agreed with expert evaluation in 87.5% of sessions.
AI.motivation: Existing tracking methods often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset sensors, which are costly and poorly suited to scalable tracking of the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT.
AI.method: A standard smartphone camera on a tripod captures full-body movement, a pose estimation algorithm processes the footage in real time, and an MCP backend with GPT-4o analyzes the extracted biomechanical data to assess form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity and injury risk.
AI.result: In a within-subject study of 20 participants aged 18-25, the VR condition gave higher enjoyment (3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), immersion/focus (3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03) and likelihood to recommend (3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04); confidence to continue (p = 0.15) and perceived intensity did not differ significantly. The MCP system showed 87.5% agreement with expert evaluation across 10 sessions judged by one certified trainer.
AI.conclusion: The authors position the smartphone-based system as a cost-effective, scalable feedback tool and report that VR improves enjoyment and immersion; the expert agreement rests on only 10 sessions and one trainer.

title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.

AI.tldr: Proposes TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that substantially reduces cumulative visual drift over 15 to 20 editing turns in multi-turn image editing while largely preserving base-model performance. It learns preservation corrections near the trajectory tail from the editor's own on-policy rollouts.
AI.motivation: Small unintended changes accumulate into severe drift when edited outputs are repeatedly reused, and existing remedies either alter pretrained priors through multi-turn training or rely on inference-time mechanisms that are hard to scale to foundation models.
AI.method: Keeps early denoising dynamics close to the base model and concentrates preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, learned from the editor's on-policy denoising rollouts with unchanged source content as the preservation reference, without curated ground-truth editing pairs.
AI.result: Across the FLUX, SenseNova and Qwen families, TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models through this post-training step rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.

title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
summary: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

AI.tldr: Proposes the Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution task, in which a generative video model must render an event and reason about its consequences for the world state even when they are out of view, and introduces EvoWorld as a reference baseline. EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency.
AI.motivation: Generative video models render plausible pixels but lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over event consequences, so their outputs can be visually plausible yet behaviorally static or causally inconsistent.
AI.method: A brain-renderer collaboration in which a vision-language model acts as the world brain, observing generated segments, maintaining an evolving account of the world and reasoning about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually; also introduces EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions and revisit consistency.
AI.result: EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces
summary: Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes. To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces ZETA, a vision-agent architecture that separates routing policy from action execution so that misrouting and failed perception can be told apart in scientific image analysis. On a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries, explicit routing semantics raise Qwen 3.8 segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%.
AI.motivation: Multi-tool agents conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, so a failure cannot be attributed to flawed reasoning or to failed perception, which makes them unauditable for high-stakes scientific automation.
AI.method: ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools and treats measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output; in a controlled study it isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed.
AI.result: Explicit routing-policy specification improves routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, though gains vary across models; for Qwen 3.8 segmentation routing rises from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing from 60.0% to 100%. Execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides infrastructure for isolating interpretive errors from execution errors, which the authors argue is a prerequisite for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.

title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
summary: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher this http URL across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport method for one-shot and few-round federated learning that aligns neurons and weights parameters by importance when merging client models. It reports consistent improvements over competing baselines on multiple datasets in both settings.
AI.motivation: Without frequent synchronization, client models drift apart so that neurons learning similar features occupy different positions, and data heterogeneity makes parameters differ in importance, so direct averaging mismatches neurons and gives equal weight to unequally important parameters.
AI.method: Uses Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters by alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, FedFiOT consistently outperforms competing baselines in one-shot and few-round federated learning. Theoretically, the optimization monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and admits a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher information.
AI.conclusion: Fisher-weighted optimal transport provides a principled way to align and aggregate client models in communication-efficient federated learning, backed by a stationarity bound.

title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to the ARC Prize 2026 paper track. Code: this https URL
summary: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.

AI.tldr: Introduces SARBLOH, an open-weight ARC-AGI-3 agent built on a zero-parameter perception engine that turns each frame into an object inventory, a geometric briefing and an annotated canvas, paired with a code-as-action runtime. Grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 while cutting token use by 89.4%.
AI.motivation: Frontier models that read raw integer grids lose spatial topology and spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries, and ARC-AGI-3 penalizes exploratory waste quadratically, so the authors ask whether perception rather than planning governs performance.
AI.method: A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine processes each frame in 35 ms into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas; the code-as-action runtime lets the agent write algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves.
AI.result: Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency and Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%; on the hidden Kaggle evaluation SARBLOH scored 16.53, 13.7 times the first Milestone winner.
AI.conclusion: Spatial perception rather than planning capacity appears to govern interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3, though active verification probes remain necessary because single-frame affordance guesses are unreliable.

title: Message-passing graph persistence
summary: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test. Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors that can complement GNN representations, but existing approaches typically compute persistence separately from the representation learning process. In this paper, we introduce Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations. At each filtration step, node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events. These embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation. We prove that MGP is invariant under graph isomorphism and that it is strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends. We evaluate MGP on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets. Experiments show that MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of these datasets.

AI.tldr: Introduces Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations so node embeddings are updated during persistence computation. The authors prove MGP is isomorphism-invariant and strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends, and it outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most evaluated datasets.
AI.motivation: Message-passing GNNs are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test, and persistent homology can complement them, but existing approaches compute persistence separately from representation learning.
AI.method: At each filtration step node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events, and these embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation.
AI.result: Evaluated on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets, MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of them.
AI.conclusion: Coupling message passing with persistent homology yields topological descriptors that are provably more expressive than the PH-based descriptors they extend.

title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
summary: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

AI.tldr: Presents a toolchain for developing ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGAs from high-level code, implementing a Vitis HLS to HDK to AFI bridge with a four-level debugging methodology. It implements the embedding layer and first encoder layer of a fine-tuned TinyBERT on the FPGA, and performance is poor compared with CPU and GPU implementations.
AI.motivation: Despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability, the academic literature has lacked a complete Vitis HLS to AFI workflow for ML development on cloud FPGAs.
AI.method: A four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) localizes errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors, and lets coding agents implement and debug FPGA designs; the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies and HLS engineering decisions are documented.
AI.result: TinyBERT fine-tuned for address named entity recognition has its embedding layer and first of four encoder layers implemented on the FPGA. The implementation streams weights from host DRAM and yields poor performance compared with CPU and GPU implementations.
AI.conclusion: The toolchain makes high-level-language FPGA development on AWS possible in practice, and the authors discuss forward paths to address the weight-streaming bottleneck.

title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
summary: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.

AI.tldr: Trains context-answer metamodels that forecast the mean-pooled answer activations of a language model from the activations produced while reading the context, before the first answer token is generated. The forecasts reach high fidelity, generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain data, retain behavior-predictive signal, and transfer across model families.
AI.motivation: Under stochastic decoding a single context can elicit many different answers, and characterizing this variation normally requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization.
AI.method: Context-answer metamodels map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations; four metamodel families are studied, trained on sets of up to 500,000 prompts.
AI.result: All four families forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets. Context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4.
AI.conclusion: Context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of LLM behavior before the first answer token, and activation forecasts may transfer across models.

title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
summary: Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol that scores the same query-gallery task under full-image, foreground-only and shortcut-only views to show whether an identification relies on animal features or shortcuts. The authors release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and the code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.
AI.motivation: High retrieval accuracy in automated individual animal identification does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts such as background or silhouette.
AI.method: The same query-gallery retrieval task is run under full-image, foreground-only and shortcut-only views, which together turn a single retrieval score into an evidence profile.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numerical results; it states that the protocol shows how well a model performs on original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal is recoverable once the animal is removed.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval scores should be read together with an evidence profile, and the released masks and code are meant to support this evaluation across datasets.

title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 GlobalSouthAI Workshop
summary: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.

AI.tldr: Shows that pedestrian occlusion can be detected from the disagreement between apparent height and monocular metric depth, with no training and no occlusion labels, reaching AUC 0.909 on KITTI for heavy occlusion. Within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925, where true distance alone is near chance.
AI.motivation: Occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have, and a detector trained on German roads lost half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria.
AI.method: Compares the ordering of apparent height, which occlusion leaves largely unchanged, with monocular metric depth, which is pulled toward the occluder; only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition checkable without labels.
AI.result: AUC 0.909 on KITTI for heavy occlusion (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), AUC 0.894-0.925 within fixed distance bands where true distance alone is near chance, and 0.819 on synthetic CARLA scenes against 0.644 for distance alone. Depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation and attention did not improve detection outside their training distribution in the configurations tested.
AI.conclusion: Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.

title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
comment: Code and videos at: this https URL
summary: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See this https URL for code and videos.

AI.tldr: Presents HALO, a humanoid autonomy system trained on vision-language-motion data synthesized across a thousand procedurally generated homes, which transfers zero-shot to real environments with a 91% success rate over 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. It orchestrates learned skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Generalist humanoid autonomy is limited by a data bottleneck, since no large corpus pairs pixels and free-form language with low-level joint commands, and teleoperation or wearable capture needs at least an hour of human time per hour of data.
AI.method: A pipeline synthesizes vision-language-motion data across procedurally generated homes so the corpus scales with compute rather than human labor; the system acquires skills such as sitting, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes, and orchestrates them.
AI.result: Without seeing a real home during training, HALO achieves a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that compute-scaled synthetic data can support zero-shot transfer of humanoid autonomy to physical homes without human-collected training data.

title: Generalized Hyperrectangular Prediction Sets in Multivariate Conformal Prediction
summary: In multivariate conformal prediction, many nonconformity scores yield prediction sets with complex geometry (e.g., ellipsoids or density level sets) that are difficult to interpret and visualize. Hyperrectangles offer a practical alternative by providing one interval per output. We extend this notion to Cartesian products of arbitrary one-dimensional sets, which we call generalized hyperrectangles. We introduce a rectangularization framework that turns any continuous multivariate nonconformity score, or conditional density, into one yielding generalized hyperrectangular prediction sets with finite-sample coverage. We establish key geometric properties of our rectangularization framework and provide useful intuitions on generalized hyperrectangles. We further establish a representation theorem showing that a broad class of hyperrectangular conformal methods based on max-aggregated coordinate-wise scores can be interpreted as rectangularizations of implicit conditional densities. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we quantify the efficiency cost of rectangularization, while highlighting its benefits, especially for practical applications of uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: Introduces generalized hyperrectangles, which are Cartesian products of arbitrary one-dimensional sets, and a rectangularization framework that turns any continuous multivariate nonconformity score or conditional density into one yielding such prediction sets with finite-sample coverage.
AI.motivation: Prediction sets from many multivariate conformal scores, such as ellipsoids or density level sets, are hard to interpret and visualize, while ordinary hyperrectangles give one interval per output but are restricted to intervals.
AI.method: A rectangularization framework applied to any continuous multivariate nonconformity score or conditional density, with its geometric properties established and a representation theorem showing that hyperrectangular methods based on max-aggregated coordinate-wise scores can be read as rectangularizations of implicit conditional densities.
AI.result: Synthetic and real-world experiments quantify the efficiency cost of rectangularization while highlighting its benefits for uncertainty quantification; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Rectangularization offers interpretable multivariate prediction sets with finite-sample coverage at a quantifiable efficiency cost, which is useful for practical uncertainty quantification.

title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
summary: Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts.
