AI.tldr: SRRM is a lightweight, reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates targeted retrieval and global information reconstruction for small language models, together with the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR). On Qwen2.5 models, reconstruction degrades much faster than retrieval as context grows, and the 1.5B model outperforms the 3B model.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mainly test retrieval, which gives limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation in small language models deployed on consumer hardware.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs Targeted Retrieval with Global Information Reconstruction on a synthetic dataset of 10 to 100 factual statements, and defines MPR as a benchmark-level metric relating retrieval and reconstruction performance. It is evaluated on Qwen2.5 models with 0.5B, 1.5B and 3B parameters.
AI.result: Qwen2.5-1.5B achieves the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%) and MPR (0.53). Qwen2.5-3B reaches 72.2% retrieval, 18.5% reconstruction and an MPR of 0.26. Reconstruction falls substantially faster than retrieval as context increases.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval alone is insufficient to characterise long-context memory, and a larger parameter count does not necessarily improve memory preservation; SRRM offers a reproducible and extensible way to reveal behaviour hidden under retrieval-only evaluation.

title: Rewrite, Then Veto: Rewriter-Agnostic Edit Gating for LLM-Based Post-OCR Correction
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL models: this https URL
summary: LLMs can repair noisy OCR transcripts of historical documents, but they also change text that was already correct. We propose EditVeto, a veto gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, its differences are split into blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block. An oracle analysis motivates the design: given the true error locations, per-span generation is worse than no correction, whereas vetoing a full rewrite's edits helps. Trained on rewrites by two Qwen3 models and evaluated, frozen, on the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the gate improves all five rewriters tested, two of them unseen in training: weighted cMER falls by 0.0026-0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15-0.25 (paired bootstrap, p ~ 0.0002 each). On published competition outputs it lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). In a second, disclosed test look, a retrained gate still improves LoRA-tuned rewriters (cMER -0.0011 to -0.0021), and an ensemble of their gated edits reaches a cMER of 0.0069 and a preference score of 0.928, mostly through fine-tuning and pooling rather than gating. Built only on public models and data, it is behind the winner (0.0050) and tied with the second-ranked run (0.0071), both from the only team using domain pre-training, and ahead of all other published runs. A third, secondary look shows the unchanged gate improving zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B (cMER 0.0114 to 0.0108) but only the preference score of its LoRA-tuned version.

AI.tldr: EditVeto is a 0.6B-parameter gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite of OCR text. It splits the rewrite's character-aligned differences into blocks and keeps or reverts each one, and it improves all five rewriters tested, including two unseen in training, by lowering weighted cMER and raising the preference score.
AI.motivation: LLMs can repair noisy OCR transcripts of historical documents, but they also alter text that was already correct, so an edit control mechanism is needed.
AI.method: A veto gate is trained on rewrites from two Qwen3 models and evaluated frozen on the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, its differences are split into blocks, and the gate decides for each block whether to keep or revert it. An oracle analysis shows that vetoing a full rewrite's edits helps, while per-span generation given true error locations is worse than no correction.
AI.result: Weighted cMER falls by 0.0026 to 0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15 to 0.25 across the five rewriters (paired bootstrap, p about 0.0002 each). On published competition outputs the gate lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). In a second test look, an ensemble of gated LoRA-tuned edits reaches cMER 0.0069 and a preference score of 0.928, and is tied with the second-ranked run (0.0071).
AI.conclusion: The gate is rewriter-agnostic and helps in most settings, though the best overall gains mostly come from fine-tuning and pooling rather than from gating, and the winning run remains ahead (0.0050).

title: RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking
summary: Different retrievers exist for retrieval-augmented generation, yet none performs best for all queries. Therefore, the key question is: given a query and retrieved passages from different retrievers, which one is most suited for that query? Existing routers usually make predictions from query-specific features and a fixed pool of retrievers; such routers have no output for an unseen retriever and are incapable by design on a new corpus. To fill these gaps, RAGCompass reads the retrieved passage sets themselves: passages from an unfamiliar retriever or corpus stay directly comparable to other passages, so routing stays well designed where a query-only map would fail. We contrastively fine-tune a reranker against the answer each evidence set produces, which accounts for most of the gain; a small comparison head adds a moderate improvement, and neither component has retriever-specific parameters. RAGCompass improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever, and outperforms fusion baselines, three query-only routers, and a prompted 8B language model. Generalization experiments show that RAGCompass keeps most of its gain under an unseen corpus, retriever, or reader, while query-only baselines fall to the best fixed retriever or below.

AI.tldr: RAGCompass routes each query to the most suitable retriever by reranking the retrieved passage sets themselves, rather than relying on query features. It improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever and keeps most of its gain under an unseen corpus, retriever or reader.
AI.motivation: No single retriever is best for every query, and existing routers rely on query-specific features over a fixed pool of retrievers, so they cannot produce outputs for an unseen retriever and fail on a new corpus.
AI.method: A reranker is contrastively fine-tuned against the answer that each evidence set produces, which accounts for most of the gain, and a small comparison head adds a moderate improvement. Neither component has retriever-specific parameters, so passages from unfamiliar retrievers remain directly comparable.
AI.result: RAGCompass improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever and outperforms fusion baselines, three query-only routers and a prompted 8B language model. Under an unseen corpus, retriever or reader it keeps most of its gain, while query-only baselines fall to the best fixed retriever or below.
AI.conclusion: Routing based on the retrieved evidence sets generalises better than query-only routing, offering a practical way to select retrievers for new corpora and retrievers.

title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
summary: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a speech transcription interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for uncertain concepts, initially for French and Spanish functional utterances. It is a planned study and reports no results yet.
AI.motivation: Transcription errors are hard to notice when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar, so listeners need help recovering the speaker's intended action.
AI.method: The interface combines alternative transcripts, audio replay and pictograms checked against context for selected uncertain concepts. A counterbalanced study will compare pictorial feedback with text alternatives alone, and will also measure semantic mismatch and extra interaction time.
AI.result: No results are reported; the abstract states the study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the intended action beyond text alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The authors aim to determine whether pictograms repair ASR errors, while noting that an inappropriate image could reinforce the wrong interpretation.

title: Cognitive Bias Signatures in Search-Equipped LLM Agents: A Stage-Resolved Analysis
summary: Search can help LLM agents correct mistakes, but their starting conditions may shape which evidence they find and use. Drawing on cognitive-bias paradigms, we develop a controlled search harness to examine result order, records of prior work, and initial hypotheses while holding each question and document collection fixed. Matched controls distinguish order effects from differences in document composition and the effects of failed work from context length. Across 10 models and 1,000 synthetic search worlds, we track queries, retrieved documents, document openings, and final answers. Our comparisons suggest that final answers are more sensitive to initial evidence order during active search than when all evidence is supplied in full. Dead-end histories can reduce strategy switching relative to matched neutral histories, indicating an effect beyond context length. Under wrong hypotheses, stage measurements distinguish reduced retrieval or opening from errors that persist after counter-evidence is opened. Exploratory interventions show that opening counter-evidence more often can coincide with lower accuracy, while accuracy can improve with little change in opening.

AI.tldr: Across 10 models and 1,000 synthetic search worlds, final answers are more sensitive to initial evidence order during active search than when all evidence is supplied in full, and dead-end histories reduce strategy switching beyond the effect of context length. The paper traces cognitive biases through the stages of search: retrieval, opening, and persistence of errors.
AI.motivation: Starting conditions such as result order, records of prior work and initial hypotheses may shape which evidence search agents find and use, and the effects need to be separated from document composition and context length.
AI.method: A controlled search harness holds each question and document collection fixed and varies result order, prior-work records and initial hypotheses, with matched controls to separate order effects from composition and failed work from context length. Queries, retrieved documents, document openings and final answers are tracked across stages.
AI.result: Dead-end histories reduce strategy switching relative to matched neutral histories. Under wrong hypotheses, stage measurements separate reduced retrieval or opening from errors that persist after counter-evidence is opened. Opening counter-evidence more often can coincide with lower accuracy, while accuracy can improve with little change in opening.
AI.conclusion: Initial conditions affect search agents through distinct stages, so stage-resolved analysis is needed to understand why search-equipped agents make errors.

title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
summary: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.

AI.tldr: Pro-Memory is a memory framework for proactive LLM agents that keeps future-directed intentions separate from the decision of when and how to act on them. It outperforms representative memory approaches on delayed-intention and proactive assistance benchmarks across several LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.
AI.motivation: Most agent memory systems are retrospective, but proactive agents also need prospective memory to retain intentions and realise them at the right opportunity, which requires more than remembering the intention.
AI.method: Pending objectives are stored with their supporting evidence, and new observations are assessed against the original goals and activation conditions. Intention states are updated from actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, and an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions.
AI.result: Experiments on two benchmarks, covering delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance, show consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, with fewer unnecessary interventions.
AI.conclusion: Separating the maintenance of intentions from their timely realisation, and learning from episode feedback, makes memory more effective for proactive agents.

title: Phonological Knowledge of Chinese Characters in Language Models
summary: How much phonological knowledge do language models (LMs) possess about Chinese characters, and how is this knowledge represented and used? We introduce PinyinBench, a controlled benchmark covering homophones, phonological features (initials, finals, and tones), and polyphonic characters. We investigate 17 text-only and multimodal LMs through three complementary approaches: behavioral evaluation, layer-wise probing, and activation steering. Behaviorally, models demonstrate substantial knowledge of initials and finals, with a frontier model (DS-v4-flash) scoring 90%+ in homophone judgment, when two characters share no phonological features. However, its accuracy drops sharply to 72% when two characters differ only in lexical tone. Probing reveals that tone is highly decodable from embeddings and improves modestly across layers, whereas segmental information starts less decodable and improves substantially with depth. Activation steering shows that segmental representations can systematically influence generation, while tone exhibits much weaker effects. Furthermore, audio-bearing training improves phonological decodability, including tone, without corresponding improvements in steering effectiveness. Together, these findings reveal distinct representational and functional profiles for segmental and tonal information, with tonal information much harder to access and manipulate, demonstrating the necessity for combined evaluation, probing, and causal intervention for understanding linguistic knowledge in LMs.

AI.tldr: PinyinBench shows that LMs know initials and finals well but handle lexical tone much less well: a frontier model scores over 90% on homophone judgment when characters share no phonological features, but only 72% when they differ only in tone. Probing and activation steering confirm that tone is harder to access and manipulate than segmental information.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how much phonological knowledge of Chinese characters language models have and how that knowledge is represented and used.
AI.method: The authors introduce PinyinBench, a controlled benchmark covering homophones, phonological features (initials, finals and tones) and polyphonic characters. Seventeen text-only and multimodal LMs are studied through behavioural evaluation, layer-wise probing and activation steering.
AI.result: Models show substantial knowledge of initials and finals, and the frontier model DS-v4-flash scores 90% or more on homophone judgment without shared features, dropping to 72% when characters differ only in tone. Tone is highly decodable from embeddings and improves modestly across layers, whereas segmental information improves substantially with depth. Steering influences segmental generation systematically but has much weaker effects on tone. Audio-bearing training improves phonological decodability, including tone, without better steering.
AI.conclusion: Segmental and tonal information have distinct representational and functional profiles, with tone much harder to access and manipulate, so combined evaluation, probing and causal intervention are needed to understand linguistic knowledge in LMs.

title: TandemBench: Benchmarking Decision Models for Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Decision models choose among predefined options in tasks such as routing and action selection. In multi-agent collaboration, a decision determines how members divide work, exchange resources, and act in parallel. We introduce TandemBench, a benchmark of 1,200 questions in multi-agent cooking scenarios where coordination choices affect goal completion. Models receive complete global information and candidate team plans, with reference answers established through execution and exact search. Models select an optimal team plan and, in paired variants that retain or remove it, judge whether better arrangements exist beyond the supplied options. We evaluate 40 native decision models and compare them with 10 general-purpose language models. The best native decision model achieves 62.50% decision accuracy. Native decision models remain close to chance in optimality verification. Paired tests reveal that some report better alternatives regardless of whether an optimal plan is already present. These findings show that team-plan decision accuracy alone can conceal systematic errors in judging whether the supplied options contain an optimal arrangement. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TandemBench is a benchmark of 1,200 multi-agent cooking questions for evaluating decision models that choose team plans. The best native decision model reaches 62.50% decision accuracy, and native models stay near chance at verifying whether an optimal plan exists among the options.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent collaboration, a decision determines how members divide work, exchange resources and act in parallel, but team-plan accuracy alone may hide systematic errors in judging whether the supplied options contain an optimal arrangement.
AI.method: Models receive complete global information and candidate team plans, and reference answers come from execution and exact search. They select an optimal plan and, in paired variants that retain or remove that plan, judge whether better arrangements exist beyond the supplied options. Forty native decision models and ten general-purpose language models are compared.
AI.result: The best native decision model achieves 62.50% decision accuracy. Native decision models remain close to chance in optimality verification, and paired tests show that some report better alternatives regardless of whether an optimal plan is already present.
AI.conclusion: Team-plan decision accuracy alone can conceal systematic errors, so optimality verification should be evaluated separately; the dataset and code are public.

title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines
summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CARTBench evaluates LLM shopping advice on complex and ambiguous requests with timelines, using 1,328 expert-annotated rubric criteria across Core, Excellence and Safety. Three of ten models exceed 90% on Core, but none exceeds 45% on Excellence, which reveals an understanding-to-execution gap.
AI.motivation: Reliable evaluation of LLM shopping assistants is hindered by data scarcity and the difficulty of standardising criteria for multi-turn product recommendation.
AI.method: Cases are drawn from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, paired with timestamped dialogue and 1,603 product records. Case-specific rubrics follow Ideal Response Principles distilled from excellent replies, and these principles also guide a structured recommendation strategy, Principle-Guided CART Prompting. Seven flagship commercial API models and open-weight models of 35B+ parameters are evaluated under frozen rubrics.
AI.result: Three of ten models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Shared failures involve product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns.
AI.conclusion: Models understand required behaviour but do not yet produce high-quality purchase advice, and the diagnosed failure modes point to where improvement is needed.

title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 19 tables. Ancillary files include a public rendering of the confirmation protocol and summary results
summary: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $\Delta^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.

AI.tldr: Better error prediction in LLM-built knowledge graphs does not automatically improve audits, because the gain depends on repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Under ideal repair on Re-DocRED, an error-rate times fan-out queue leaves 3.98 to 4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint planner with the same actions.
AI.motivation: Confidence estimates guide human review of LLM-built knowledge graphs, yet better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit, and the reason for this gap needs to be characterised.
AI.method: Non-adaptive auditing is modelled as budgeted covering, the minimal decision-relevant error statistics are characterised, and the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning is bounded by a structural mass. Ideal repair is simulated against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, with frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents.
AI.result: On the held-out graphs, the error-rate times fan-out queue leaves 3.98 to 4.74 percentage points more errors than the joint model. Opening shared actions for the joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89 to 1.43 points relative to its fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models is inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set.
AI.conclusion: Audit gains depend on the planning model rather than on confidence quality alone, and LLM adjudication can identify possible omissions in the benchmark.

title: Information-Matched Auditing of Conversational Emotion-Shift Forecasting: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation Protocol
summary: Comparisons in conversational emotion-shift forecasting are easily distorted when a learned model receives rich features but its transition baseline is given a noisy or unavailable current-emotion label, when hyperparameter budgets differ, or when target-turn information enters the representation. We present an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol that closes these gaps with an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal four-configuration validation searches, and seed-dialogue-aware inference. Applying it to six causal model families on four text corpora and two feature-source sensitivity configurations shows that a deployable train-only current-emotion classifier feeding the transition baseline yields a different verdict than an oracle diagnostic where both sides receive gold current emotion. Under the deployable condition, learned models improve over the predicted-label baseline on all four primary corpora; DailyDialog gains are large and survive a 72-comparison Holm correction (best ROC-AUC gain = +0.167, adjusted p=.0144). Under matched gold information, the baseline remains competitive on IEMOCAP and stronger on MELD, while every model retains a large DailyDialog advantage. We additionally report precision-recall AUC, calibration, a strictly utterance-local feature control, same-person self-shift forecasting, and a future-access dose-response test. An eight-item leakage checklist accompanies the protocol. Code, raw seed predictions, and reporting artifacts are available from the corresponding author upon request.

AI.tldr: An information-matched, leakage-safe protocol shows that verdicts on conversational emotion-shift forecasting depend on whether the transition baseline receives the same current-emotion information as the learned model. Under deployable conditions learned models beat the predicted-label baseline on all four primary corpora, with a large DailyDialog gain that survives Holm correction.
AI.motivation: Comparisons in emotion-shift forecasting are easily distorted by mismatched information, unequal hyperparameter budgets and target-turn leakage, so a fair audit protocol is needed.
AI.method: The protocol adds an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal four-configuration validation searches and seed-dialogue-aware inference. It is applied to six causal model families on four text corpora and two feature-source sensitivity configurations, comparing a train-only current-emotion classifier with an oracle that gives both sides gold current emotion.
AI.result: Under the deployable condition, learned models improve over the predicted-label baseline on all four primary corpora, and DailyDialog gains survive a 72-comparison Holm correction (best ROC-AUC gain +0.167, adjusted p=.0144). Under matched gold information the baseline remains competitive on IEMOCAP and stronger on MELD, while every model retains a large DailyDialog advantage.
AI.conclusion: The verdict depends on the information condition, so reported gains in emotion-shift forecasting should be checked against matched baselines and an explicit leakage checklist.

title: Selective, Risk-Controlled Emotion Forecasting in Conversation: From a Persistence Barrier to Departure Detection with Conformal Guarantees
summary: Forecasting emotion in conversation is increasingly framed as predicting the next emotional state's value. We show this targets a hard quantity in a state-observed testbed and propose a learnable, deployable reformulation instead. On valence-arousal-dominance trajectories from a dyadic corpus, repeating a speaker's own previous state sets a persistence baseline that no frozen-encoder correction meaningfully improves upon and a state-space filter exceeds; the floor requires the historical state to be observed, since an estimated anchor collapses persistence below a direct forecaster. What survives is the timing of a departure from persistence, learnable on three of four corpora and near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus, a negative result we report. We recast the task as selective departure forecasting: a lead-time-weighted metric with a leakage protocol, and commitment policies whose best choice switches with the departure rate. A dialogue-level conformal risk control bounds the expected loss of committed predictions, meeting the target in all twelve configurations tested, though the guarantee is bought through abstention, with coverage and alarm recall falling sharply on the hardest corpus. One tested language model's confidence fails as a ranking signal where another succeeds, a model-dependent failure not yet attributable to family versus scale. Code and result logs are available from the corresponding author upon request.

AI.tldr: Emotion forecasting in conversation is reframed as selective departure forecasting, which predicts when an emotional state will leave persistence and is supported by dialogue-level conformal risk control. Repeating the speaker's previous state is a strong persistence baseline, and the departure timing is learnable on three of four corpora but near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus.
AI.motivation: Forecasting the next emotional state's value targets a hard quantity, since persistence of the previous state sets a baseline that frozen-encoder corrections barely improve on.
AI.method: The task is recast as selective departure forecasting, with a lead-time-weighted metric, a leakage protocol and commitment policies whose best choice depends on the departure rate. Dialogue-level conformal risk control bounds the expected loss of committed predictions, on valence-arousal-dominance trajectories from a dyadic corpus.
AI.result: Persistence is not meaningfully improved by frozen-encoder correction, and a state-space filter exceeds it, but only when the historical state is observed. Departure timing is learnable on three of four corpora and near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus. The conformal control meets the target in all twelve configurations tested, but only through abstention, with coverage and alarm recall falling sharply on the hardest corpus. One language model's confidence fails as a ranking signal where another succeeds.
AI.conclusion: The reformulation is more learnable and deployable than value forecasting, though its guarantees require substantial abstention, and the model-dependence of confidence remains unexplained.

title: Familiar letters, not related languages, let unseen languages into a shared space of meaning
summary: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and whether a model learning one from untranslated text builds on a related language or familiar letters is unclear: they usually coincide. Here we show that familiar letters, not a related language, let an unseen language into a shared space of meaning. GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and lets any sentence be shown in any script, was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter although its close relative Thai was in pretraining; Santali, which had none, entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script. Transliteration into familiar scripts may thus open multilingual models to languages without translations.

AI.tldr: GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels, retrieves English translations for untranslated Lao seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Unseen languages enter the shared meaning space through familiar letters rather than through a related language.
AI.motivation: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and it is unclear whether a model learning from untranslated text relies on a related language or on familiar letters, since these usually coincide.
AI.method: GlyphMind is pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems, then adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen. Tests compare Lao in its own script, Lao rewritten in unfamiliar letters, and Santali, which has no pretraining data, in Devanagari and in its own script.
AI.result: Adapted on untranslated Lao, GlyphMind retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter the shared space even though its close relative Thai was in pretraining. Santali entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script.
AI.conclusion: Transliteration into familiar scripts may open multilingual models to languages without translations, indicating that script familiarity can matter more than linguistic relatedness.

title: Holistic Parallel Supervision for Expressive Speech to Speech Translation
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), yet existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. Consequently, current systems often rely on indirect conditioning or transfer mechanisms. To obtain this supervision, we introduce a training-data construction strategy that combines professional dubbing, which provides human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. We evaluate this supervision using existing expressive S2ST systems and DirectS2ST, an end-to-end method developed in this work that predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech. Experiments on English-German and English-Spanish show that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realization across all evaluated systems. DirectS2ST exhibits the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness. To our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST.

AI.tldr: The paper builds training data that aligns source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing and speaker identity by combining professional dubbing with multilingual voice conversion. It also introduces DirectS2ST, an end-to-end model, and shows that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive speech-to-speech translation on English-German and English-Spanish.
AI.motivation: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation, but existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly across content, prosody, timing and speaker identity, so current systems depend on indirect conditioning or transfer.
AI.method: Professional dubbing supplies human-performed correspondence in content, prosody and timing, and multilingual voice conversion reduces speaker mismatch. The supervision is evaluated with existing expressive S2ST systems and with DirectS2ST, which predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech.
AI.result: Holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realisation across all evaluated systems on English-German and English-Spanish. DirectS2ST shows the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity and human-rated expressiveness.
AI.conclusion: This is the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST, and it suggests that data construction is a key lever for expressive translation.

title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
summary: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.

AI.tldr: In a controlled case of numerical choice between 1 and 30, activation patching in Qwen3-4B shows that a pre-answer edit changes the chosen number from 17 to 15, and that its influence persists on the second digit through later computation. The study does not establish the origin or the complete circuit of numerical preference.
AI.motivation: Language models can favour particular numbers even when every integer in the range is valid, and the way preference is processed across layers and tokens is not well understood.
AI.method: Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, selective cache and attention-output replacements are used to trace the edit's continuing influence, and retrospective estimates are computed across eighteen contexts with prompt tests on held-out and fresh wordings.
AI.result: After the edit ends, selective replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs gives similar immediate readout contributions, but different final log-odds effects. Holding later MLP outputs at their edited-run values reduces the effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test, where joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap while the answer remains 17.
AI.conclusion: Later computation changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation, so numerical preference reflects persistent state and conditional downstream processing, though the complete circuit remains unestablished.

title: Adapting Qwen3 to Tajik from 0.6B to 8B: Lower Text Loss Did Not Mean Better Understanding
summary: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.

AI.tldr: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik text lower Qwen3 text loss at every size from 0.6B to 8B, but do not improve Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. The main model e3, built with continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele, with English MMLU changing by -1.2 points.
AI.motivation: Adapting language models to a low-resource language is usually judged by text loss, yet lower loss may not mean better understanding of the language.
AI.method: LoRA adapters are trained on Tajik news and books at sizes from 0.6B to 8B. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text is followed by supervised fine-tuning, and the same heavy recipe is applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base. Fifteen trained models and five starting models are scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals.
AI.result: Adapters lowered Tajik text loss by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points, while the 0.6B score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance. At 8B, continued pretraining gave a Belebele gain of 9.9 points, and after supervised fine-tuning e3 is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B, with English MMLU changing by -1.2 points. The 0.6B heavy recipe reached near-8B text loss but stayed near chance on multiple choice and lost 7.6 points on English MMLU.
AI.conclusion: Lower text loss did not translate into better understanding of Tajik, and the authors also document lost training records, undocumented data and a 4-bit release missing transformer layers.

title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
comment: Accepted and published to the ACL GEM workshop. Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM), pages 364-377, San Diego, California, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

AI.tldr: SAUCE is a reference-free, fact-based pipeline for evaluating cross-lingual conversational speech summaries by checking entailment between the conversation and the summary. It is explainable because it maps scores to discrete, verifiable facts, and preliminary results show strong alignment with human judgment.
AI.motivation: Conversations without a clear end goal are hard to summarize and evaluate, and black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics do not show which facts are hallucinated or omitted.
AI.method: The pipeline measures summary accuracy and fact coverage through entailment between the conversation and the summary text, scoring against discrete facts, and it is compared with several popular summarization metrics.
AI.result: SAUCE captures information loss caused by transcription and translation errors and identifies broken summaries better than the compared metrics, and preliminary investigations show strong alignment with human judgment.
AI.conclusion: The interpretability of SAUCE lets developers profile LLM behaviour systematically and gives end users a practical tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions.

title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.

AI.tldr: LooM is a loop-invariant memory design for causal encoder-decoder language models that loops only the decoder layers after the first, so the KV cache does not grow with the loop count. A single model trained on random loop budgets covers budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token and outperforms a single-pass baseline when given enough loops.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers increase effective depth but suffer from memory that grows with the loop count, compute that can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and a loop count that is hard to change after training.
AI.method: In a causal encoder-decoder, the decoder layers after the first read a global memory written once per token, and each looping layer publishes its key-value entry only on its first visit; the layers loop independently and are trained on randomly sampled budgets without a router.
AI.result: With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size; the training budget distribution is shown to determine what extra depth buys.
AI.conclusion: A causal encoder-decoder is a natural place to loop because memory is written once and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment rather than fixed at training.

title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
summary: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

AI.tldr: TASC is a benchmark of 3,418 conversational inputs for testing whether LLM assistants apply time-dependent safety constraints that users do not restate in later requests. Across 13 models, the assistants apply such constraints in only 30.5% of violating cases, and they fail in 62.1% of cases even when they calculate the elapsed time correctly.
AI.motivation: LLM assistants help with everyday activities that have time-dependent constraints, but users may not repeat those constraints later in a conversation, so assistants must recognize and adjust their advice on their own.
AI.method: TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, plus a separate set of 33 scenarios that compare a model's ability to calculate elapsed time with its ability to apply that information.
AI.result: Assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule while rarely warning users unnecessarily; models fail to apply the constraints in 62.1% of cases despite computing the elapsed time correctly, and explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
summary: Common methods for monitoring features in large language models (LLMs) such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features maintain a consistent representation across contexts. LLMs, however, can flexibly adopt different perspectives or "personas" that suggest different underlying systems of conceptual relations. In this paper, we examine whether prompting an LLM to adopt a persona alters the representational geometry of the model's latent space. We extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare these against two neutral baselines. We find that persona conditioning systematically alters both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes themselves in directions consistent with the specified ideology. We then test the implications of this reorganization for two safety-relevant features: truthfulness and morality. Linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and classifiers built from manually selected word representations, all trained without a persona, produce divergent results when applied to models conditioned on political personas, producing politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements. These findings suggest that internal representations, as they are conventionally extracted, can exhibit different geometric relations when the model adopts personas, potentially undermining monitoring efforts.

AI.tldr: Prompting an LLM to adopt a liberal or conservative political persona systematically reorganizes the geometry of its latent representations. Probes, SAE-based classifiers and manually selected word representations trained without a persona then give politically slanted truth and morality ratings.
AI.motivation: Common feature monitoring methods such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders assume that features keep a consistent representation across contexts, yet LLMs can flexibly adopt personas that imply different systems of conceptual relations.
AI.method: The authors extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare them with two neutral baselines, then test the effect on the safety-relevant features of truthfulness and morality.
AI.result: Persona conditioning changes both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes in directions consistent with the specified ideology, and classifiers trained without a persona produce divergent and politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements.
AI.conclusion: Internal representations as conventionally extracted can show different geometric relations under personas, which could undermine monitoring efforts.

title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
comment: 29 pages. Authors' version of the open access article published in Information Sciences (CC BY 4.0). This version corrects the second affiliation of Marco Polignano (Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg); the published version lists the European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC) in error. Marco Polignano is not affiliated with the JRC. No other content has been changed
summary: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

AI.tldr: This empirical benchmark on the MTEB shows that int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, while binary quantization is significantly worse. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 gives a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical text embeddings and quantization both aim to improve efficiency, but how these two established techniques interact had not been systematically measured.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 38 MTEB tasks with four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit and binary quantization for 168 configurations per task, reporting theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time separately and analysing results with a Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc analysis.
AI.result: Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above m=16 while two successive halvings always are; no evidence shows that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially; retrieval degrades far faster than other task categories.
AI.conclusion: Findings should be reported per task category, since the efficiency and effectiveness trade-offs differ strongly across categories, and evaluation times were measured once and are only indicative.

title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
summary: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.

AI.tldr: SpecCompact speeds up LLM agent context compaction by generating structured summary slots in parallel with a fine-tuned small drafter and verifying them with the target model. It achieves 2.04 to 5.63 times compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization on AppWorld and tau^3 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Summarizing long agent interaction histories with large models adds substantial latency, so compaction must balance information retention against speed.
AI.method: The framework uses slot-parallel semantic speculative verification: a small drafter fine-tuned for the task generates structured summary slots in parallel, the target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix, and system optimizations reduce repeated context processing and model calls.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and tau^3 with two target models, SpecCompact achieves 2.04 to 5.63 times compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization, separate downstream evaluations show model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs, and a user study within Hermes shows an 8.68 times median compaction speedup.
AI.conclusion: Speculative slot generation is a practical way to cut compaction latency for LLM agents, though its downstream quality effects depend on the model and task.

title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
summary: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.

AI.tldr: turing-unlock is a kernel module that lifts the driver-level throttling of FP16 tensor throughput on the RTX 2080 Ti, and the authors measure its effect on from-scratch pre-training of five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models. The throughput gain rises with model size, reaching +11.8% for the small tier, with bit-identical peak memory and consistent final quality.
AI.motivation: The RTX 2080 Ti has full second-generation Tensor Cores, but the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication in the driver, so usable tensor throughput stays well below the hardware peak.
AI.method: The kernel module writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex before the nvidia driver binds the device, and the before-and-after throughput is measured under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as a companion memory study (five tiers, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42).
AI.result: The small tier (75.7M parameters) rises from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h; the tiny tier gains +4.7%; the pico-micro tiers gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. Published cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rises from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x).
AI.conclusion: The unlock gain is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched and grows monotonically with matrix size, so it is negligible for the smallest tiers and a double-digit percentage at the small tier.

title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
summary: Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet -- and across numerous measurement techniques -- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

AI.tldr: Across single-word (N = 40,000) and multi-word (N = 67,000) concepts, more abstract concepts are more associated with men in internet text and images, and LLMs reproduce this male abstraction bias in free association tasks. The bias maps onto grammar, with verbs and adverbs being more abstract and more male-coded.
AI.motivation: Abstractness and gender are usually studied as separable features of human cognition, but the authors ask whether they are systematically linked across the whole conceptual space.
AI.method: The authors measure the association between abstractness and gender across billions of words and millions of images on the internet using numerous measurement techniques, replicate the pattern in languages around the world, and examine human and AI responses in free association tasks.
AI.result: More abstract concepts are more associated with men across conceptual domains, the pattern extends to verbs and adverbs, which are more abstract and more male-coded, and the bias appears in both human and AI free association responses.
AI.conclusion: The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of gender stereotypes, indicating that gender is a core organizing dimension of conceptual space and that it is internalized and algorithmically reproduced.

title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MAEP is a training-free expert pruning method for MoE multimodal LLMs that scores expert importance separately for vision and text tokens in a single forward pass. On three MoE-based MLLMs it outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks and cuts about 27 GB of BF16 expert weights, letting a roughly 58 GB model fit on one 40 GB GPU.
AI.motivation: Expert parameters account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs, and existing expert pruning methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision and language processing.
AI.method: MAEP introduces Delta-H Output, a redistribution-aware metric that measures the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and low-attention vision tokens as a dataset-stable pruning signal; text-side importance is used as a preservation signal, vision-side importance as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers.
AI.result: MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) on InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and a third MoE-MLLM.
AI.conclusion: Modality-aware pruning makes large MoE-MLLMs fit on a single 40 GB GPU with limited loss of capability, and the code is publicly released.

title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
summary: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

AI.tldr: Two multimodal LLMs, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, judge which of paired Seoul street images feels safer when robots are present or absent, and their choices are compared with 25 human respondents. Both models prefer streets without robots and favour a delivery robot over a humanoid, and robots are chosen more often at night.
AI.motivation: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street was unclear.
AI.method: The authors generate 18 images of Seoul streets varying in time of day, road class and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid), and have Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B choose the safer image in each pair under persona conditioning, with the same task given to human respondents.
AI.result: Both models prefer streets without robots and favour the delivery robot over the humanoid; robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, while road class has smaller effects; the model rationales describe the delivery robot as a physical obstacle and the humanoid as either a threat or protection, and Gemma shows a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans.
AI.conclusion: The effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.

AI.tldr: SimpleHC simplifies Hyper-Connections by removing residual mixing and sharing memory access, and it stays comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models while adding only 2.4% training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. The analysis shows that learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates each achieve performance comparable to mHC.
AI.motivation: Hyper-Connections are increasingly used in frontier language models, but their components are poorly understood and they add non-negligible training overhead.
AI.method: The authors study the HC architecture component by component, identify two effective interaction groups, and identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a source of overhead; SimpleHC uses layer-specific gates that share a group-entry state for batched reads and deferred writes, and scalar corrections that preserve preceding sublayer output contributions.
AI.result: SimpleHC maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, shows smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, remains stable under stress, and incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale.
AI.conclusion: Simpler and more efficient designs can match sophisticated residual architectures at scale, making performance gains more accessible for foundation model training.

title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
summary: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior-capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($\rho = 0.945$), while joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) through a behavior-capability frontier that maximizes behavioral gain under an explicit bound on capability loss. Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data (rho = 0.945), but interventions that satisfy protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities.
AI.motivation: Activation steering can change model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not show that an intervention is usable, since CAA may degrade unrelated capabilities.
AI.method: The authors select CAA interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3% and 5% (absolute percentage points), and test them with control experiments, representational geometry analysis, secondary capability benchmarks, out-of-distribution tests and open-ended evaluations.
AI.result: Joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited further gain at 5%; effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic perturbations; representational geometry is only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering is a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first.
