The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.

AI.tldr: The paper reads model collapse as Rogers' paradox, arguing that a population relying on copying is no better off than one that never copied because copies go stale unless people keep learning for themselves. Rogers' model fitted to fully synthetic training predicts how much rare knowledge language models retain under other data mixtures, and the model is shown to be exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to verify.
AI.motivation: The theory of model collapse treats the supply of fresh outside data as a fixed archive from a fixed distribution, which the authors argue is the actual problem, and cultural evolution theory has a model of this supply.
AI.method: The authors test Rogers' model in three steps: fitting it to fully synthetic training and predicting retention of rare knowledge from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer; varying how fast the world changes for lineages that copy their own past versus restart from fixed pretrained weights; and closing the loop so that people who write training data can ask the model, making fresh data endogenous.
AI.result: Predictions fit retention within a few percentage points across mixtures of fresh data; a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data the faster the world changes, while a lineage restarting from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated; at equilibrium every increase in model-written text must be matched by more people learning for themselves.
AI.conclusion: Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox, and only checks that carry new information act as critical learning, whereas filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse.

title: SVGFaith: A Two-Layer Meta-Evaluation of Faithfulness Metrics for Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Text-to-SVG systems are commonly evaluated by applying raster-image metrics to rasterised outputs, yet whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness remains unclear. We introduce SVGFaith, a two-layer meta-evaluation framework in which the more faithful candidate of each pair is determined by construction or by human judgment. SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes, split evenly between two directions: two renderings compared against one prompt, and two descriptions compared against one rendering. SVGFaith-Arena contains 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs. On SVGFaith-Diagnostic, CLIP and three other image--text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5. We further introduce SVGFaith-Score, an interpretable pointwise metric. A domain-tuned decomposer turns each prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a visual question answering model scores whether each requirement is satisfied, and a requirement's score is discounted when its prerequisites score low. In addition to the overall score, the per-requirement scores show which requirements are judged unsatisfied and which inherit discounts from their prerequisites. SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge, on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions. Code and data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SVGFaith is a two-layer meta-evaluation framework for faithfulness metrics in text-to-SVG generation, built from 1,842 controlled diagnostic pairs and 1,327 human-annotated arena comparisons. Its proposed SVGFaith-Score, which decomposes prompts into dependency graphs of visual requirements, significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SVG systems are usually evaluated with raster-image metrics on rasterized outputs, and it was unclear whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness; CLIP reaches at most 0.672 pairwise accuracy on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5.
AI.method: SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes in two directions, rendering comparisons and description comparisons, and SVGFaith-Arena contains human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs; SVGFaith-Score uses a domain-tuned decomposer to build a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a VQA model to check each requirement, and discounts scores whose prerequisites score low.
AI.result: CLIP and three other image-text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding; SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions, and its per-requirement scores show which requirements are unsatisfied.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable, requirement-level scoring gives a more reliable measure of prompt faithfulness for text-to-SVG generation than existing image-text embedding metrics.

title: Growing One's AI Tools: A Paradigm of Practice-Grown Tools
summary: Professionals have long used software built for them by others. This article reports the growth of a professional computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool built by its own user, a conference interpreter without programming training. Drawing on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, the article traces how real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions. The record shows capabilities deployed on the day their need appeared and one strategy change that cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon. The article then proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools, defined by the shift from using to growing, the co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary, and it formulates three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what they and their tools achieve together.

AI.tldr: This article reports how a conference interpreter without programming training grew a computer-assisted interpreting tool over eight weeks, with 62 commits, six versions and telemetry from 133 logged sessions. It proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools and three propositions for tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners.
AI.motivation: Professionals have long used software built by others, but this article examines a tool built by its own user, and asks how assessment of practitioners should account for the tools they grow and use.
AI.method: The authors draw on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, tracing how real conference work drove the tool's development, and they define the paradigm through the shift from using to growing, co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary.
AI.result: Capabilities were deployed on the day their need appeared, and one strategy change cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what practitioners and their tools achieve together.

title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
summary: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the benefit of multi-turn agentic RL depends on the interaction budget, as measured by Pass@(K,T), with trajectory-level advantages shrinking when turn budgets tighten. It proposes BudgetMix RL, which varies interaction budgets during training and achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn agentic RL performs well on long-horizon tasks, but its gains are highly sensitive to interaction constraints, which creates deployment risk when the budget changes.
AI.method: The authors evaluate across sampling breadth K and interaction depth T via Pass@(K,T), give a preliminary discussion of process supervision signals, and introduce BudgetMix RL, which varies the interaction budget during training.
AI.result: Agentic RL does not uniformly improve single-step decision quality; its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience, and BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Budget-aware training is a practical way to reduce the deployment risks of multi-turn agentic RL, although the discussion of process supervision is preliminary.

title: Beyond accuracy: what AI assurance needs to establish in public services
summary: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

AI.tldr: An evaluation of eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics finds accuracy of 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels across unchanged repeats. The paper argues that public bodies need checks beyond aggregate accuracy before they rely on AI-produced evidence.
AI.motivation: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced classifications, summaries and assessments that inform policy and service delivery, so their reliability is a matter of public accountability, yet it is unclear what tests establish that reliance.
AI.method: The authors combine technical evaluation against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats with an analysis of 37 UK and EU policy documents, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation, and they examine how the proportion of outputs flagged for human review depends on the score-extraction procedure.
AI.result: Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding; under the implemented score-extraction procedure the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%; reporting expectations in the policy documents do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing.
AI.conclusion: Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance on AI outputs through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, with clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

AI.tldr: TurnWise is a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video understanding that gives each respond-or-wait decision its own group-relative advantage instead of one trajectory-level advantage. It outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding without a learned critic or additional rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO approaches for streaming video emphasize reward design but keep a single trajectory-level advantage across turns, which gives shared credit that can reinforce redundant replies or discourage useful follow-ups.
AI.method: Turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, and turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns so that response and waiting decisions have equal weight regardless of output length.
AI.result: The method outperforms prior RL approaches on streaming video understanding in extensive experiments, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy.
AI.conclusion: Aligning policy learning with individual streaming decisions improves streaming video RL without requiring a learned critic or extra rollouts.

title: Template Gap Reconstruction for Shell Output Simulation with Small Language Models
summary: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.

AI.tldr: Template gap reconstruction (TGR) improves shell output simulation with small language models by reusing output literals from a template bank and generating only the variable gaps autoregressively. It improves output edit similarity over full-output decoding when the optimal template covers more than 25% of the output and cuts generated tokens by 26.3% to 38.3%.
AI.motivation: Small language models can simulate shell output without executing commands, but full-output decoding forces them to predict both recurring utility structure and content that varies across executions.
AI.method: TGR supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels that are interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps; a template selector chooses the template, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding, and the template bank is built from 18.7 million outputs while five reconstruction models are trained on a held-out target environment.
AI.result: TGR improves output edit similarity over full-output decoding when the optimal template covers more than 25% of the output, performs similarly for lower-coverage outputs, and outperforms it for shorter gap sequences with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812 for shorter and longer sequences respectively, while reducing generated tokens by 26.3% to 38.3% across tokenizer families.
AI.conclusion: A reusable output structure is a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to quality.

title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project page: this https URL
summary: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: LongBanana is an expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark of 90 tasks for long-context multi-reference image synthesis, with about 32 reference images, 20 constraints and 50 evaluation items per task. The authors also propose LongBanana-Gen, where a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect workflow gives harness-dependent gains over direct generation.
AI.motivation: Agent-driven image generation must retrieve dispersed visual evidence, reject distractors, bind entities and relations, and compose one coherent image from many references, and no expert-verified benchmark existed for this long-context setting.
AI.method: Each task is instantiated with reference images and an entity-relation graph, and node, edge and whole-graph obligations are converted into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding and Global Constraint Satisfaction, with a 15% double-labeled subset used to check reliability.
AI.result: The benchmark contains 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa on the double-labeled subset; minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, and the ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair.
AI.conclusion: LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for building stronger agent-driven image-generation systems.

title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
comment: Accepted to the SocialAgent Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. 12 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes controlled context enrichment (four prompt substitution rules) and selective robustness, a validation criterion requiring insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt changes plus a directional response to decision-relevant changes, for LLM social agents. Demonstrated in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, enrichment forms produce distinct behavior patterns that vary between the two models tested.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in social simulations change behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, which threatens validity. Prior work did not define context richness and robustness in ways that support controlled comparisons of whether richer context helps.
AI.method: Controlled context enrichment substitutes prompts to add neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, or normative decision grounding. Selective robustness combines insensitivity to meaning-preserving variation with directional responses to decision-relevant changes in the social world.
AI.result: In a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, the enrichment forms yield distinct behavioral patterns, and these patterns vary between the two models tested. The framework identifies which enrichment forms produce more desirable and robust behavior.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives social simulation researchers a controlled way to test whether added context improves LLM agent validity, though the effects depend on the model.

title: Visual Forensic Detection of Fabricated Bangla News Photocards using Deep Learning
summary: In Bangladesh, much localized misinformation spreads as photocards: single-image news summaries that imitate the branding of well-known news organizations. Because the misleading message lives in the pixels rather than in machine-readable text, text-based fact-checking tools cannot see it. We recast photocard fake-news detection as visual image forgery detection. We build a dataset of 969 authentic and 1,077 fabricated Bangla photocards scraped from public Facebook pages: authentic cards from the verified pages of seventeen national television broadcasters, fabricated ones from pseudo-broadcaster pages, anonymous profiles, and public groups. Sixteen photometric and morphological transformations per image grow the corpus to 32,736 samples. A fully connected ANN reaches only about 52% accuracy, its loss stuck at ln(2) ~ 0.693, showing that flattening the image destroys the spatial cues forgery detection needs. A compact, fully batch-normalized four-block CNN with 489,954 parameters, about 1,644x smaller than the ANN, is evaluated with leakage-free stratified group five-fold cross-validation, which keeps every augmented version of a card in one fold. Under this protocol the CNN reaches 87.45% +/- 0.53% pooled accuracy from scratch and 88.75% +/- 1.55% when its classifier head is warm-started from the ANN. An ImageNet-pretrained YOLOv8n-cls backbone (1.44M parameters) fine-tuned on the same folds reaches 97.36% +/- 0.42%, marking the headroom above the compact model. We report per-class precision, recall, F1, and pooled confusion matrices, diagnose and fix a one-class collapse caused by an unnormalized classifier head, and give a manual error analysis and bias-variance diagnosis showing that the compact CNNs under-fit.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts Bangla photocard fake-news detection as visual image forgery detection and builds a dataset of 969 authentic and 1,077 fabricated cards, expanded to 32,736 samples by augmentation. A compact four-block CNN, an ImageNet-pretrained YOLOv8n-cls backbone, and an ANN baseline are compared under leakage-free cross-validation.
AI.motivation: Localized misinformation in Bangladesh spreads as photocards that imitate news brands, so the misleading content lives in pixels and text-based fact-checking tools cannot detect it.
AI.method: Authentic cards come from verified broadcaster pages and fabricated cards from pseudo-broadcaster pages, anonymous profiles and public groups, with sixteen photometric and morphological transformations per image. Models are evaluated with stratified group five-fold cross-validation so that every augmented version of a card stays in one fold.
AI.result: A fully connected ANN reaches about 52% accuracy. The compact CNN with 489,954 parameters reaches 87.45% plus or minus 0.53% from scratch and 88.75% plus or minus 1.55% with a warm-started head. The fine-tuned YOLOv8n-cls reaches 97.36% plus or minus 0.42%.
AI.conclusion: Flattening the image destroys spatial cues needed for forgery detection, and the compact CNNs under-fit, leaving headroom that a pretrained backbone closes. The authors also diagnose and fix a one-class collapse caused by an unnormalized classifier head.

title: mmHand: Toward Pixel-Level-Accuracy Hand Localization Using a Single Commodity mmWave Device
summary: The hand localization problem has been a longstanding focus due to its many applications. The task involves modeling the hand as a singular point and determining its position within a defined coordinate system. However, due to data modality limitations, existing hand localization technologies face several challenges. For example, vision-based localization raises privacy concerns, while wearable-based methods compromise user comfort. In this paper, we introduce mmHand, a new device-free, privacy-preserving dynamic hand localization system with pixel-level accuracy, using a single commodity mmWave device. We first propose a mmImage generation tool to fully extract spatial information from raw mmWave data and introduce a novel 2D image-format representation of mmWave data. Next, we design a framework that provides a new quality evaluation method and pixel space labeling for the mmWave data. Finally, we present a cross-modality spatial feature-enhanced model with high spatial feature extraction capabilities, which can accurately localize hand positions at the pixel level in the mmWave radar U-V pixel coordinate system. We evaluate the system with experiments on 12 subjects in three scenarios, and the results across four metrics demonstrate the effectiveness of our hand localization system.

AI.tldr: The paper presents mmHand, a device-free and privacy-preserving dynamic hand localization system that uses a single commodity mmWave radar to localize the hand at pixel level. It converts raw mmWave data into a 2D image-format representation and applies a cross-modality spatial feature-enhanced model.
AI.motivation: Vision-based hand localization raises privacy concerns, and wearable methods compromise user comfort, so existing technologies face data-modality limitations.
AI.method: An mmImage generation tool turns raw mmWave data into a 2D image representation that keeps spatial information. A framework provides a new quality evaluation method and pixel space labeling, and a cross-modality model with strong spatial feature extraction localizes hands in the radar U-V pixel coordinate system.
AI.result: The system was evaluated on 12 subjects in three scenarios across four metrics, and the abstract reports that the results demonstrate effectiveness. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A single commodity mmWave device can support privacy-preserving, pixel-level dynamic hand localization.

title: Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation for Low-textured Scientific Sketch Image Retrieval
summary: Low-textured sketch images are widely used in scientific applications, including wildlife conservation, archaeological illustration, and forensic composites. Learning from and retrieving such images is challenging because they lack detailed surface textures and visual variations commonly exploited by modern deep learning models. This paper proposes Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation (ART) to fine-tune pretrained models to learn effective representations for accurate sketch image retrieval. Our key observation is that sketches are particularly sensitive to image transformations, such as rotation, flipping, zooming, and stretching. While some transformations preserve their structural integrity, others may introduce distortions that hinder representation learning. Instead of randomly choosing transformations to construct fine-tuning views, ART formulates augmentation selection as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem, where transformations are treated as arms and their effectiveness is continuously evaluated through rewards. This enables ART to adaptively construct reward-guided view banks before self-supervised fine-tuning; the subsequent representation loss does not feed back to ART. On Florida manatee sketches provided by Mote Marine Laboratory, ART achieves 71.40% average Top-1 accuracy for transformed-scar retrieval, compared with 68.83% for random augmentation selection, and 55.84% for location-aware sketch retrieval, compared with 18.18% for frozen CLIP.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation (ART), which uses a multi-armed bandit to select augmentations when fine-tuning pretrained models for low-textured sketch image retrieval. On Florida manatee sketches, ART outperforms random augmentation selection and frozen CLIP.
AI.motivation: Low-textured scientific sketches lack the surface textures and visual variations that modern deep learning models usually exploit, and common transformations can distort sketch structure.
AI.method: Each transformation such as rotation, flipping, zooming or stretching is treated as an arm of a multi-armed bandit, and its effectiveness is updated from rewards. This builds reward-guided view banks before self-supervised fine-tuning, and the representation loss does not feed back into the selection.
AI.result: ART reaches 71.40% average Top-1 accuracy for transformed-scar retrieval, compared with 68.83% for random augmentation selection. For location-aware sketch retrieval it reaches 55.84%, compared with 18.18% for frozen CLIP.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, reward-guided augmentation selection helps fine-tune pretrained models for scientific sketch retrieval where random augmentation is less effective.

title: PointNDF: Cascaded Neural Displacement Fields for Point Cloud Denoising
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted to MMM 2027 (33rd International Conference on Multimedia Modeling)
summary: Point cloud denoising aims to recover clean geometry from noisy 3D observations while preserving both fine surface details and the underlying spatial distribution of the points. Many learning-based methods adopt a two-stage pipeline that first extracts point-wise features from the noisy input and subsequently predicts point-wise displacements via simple regressions. However, these approaches often lack robust feature guidance and distribution-aware geometric refinement, causing them to fail at maintaining optimal point uniformity and geometric quality. To address these limitations, we propose PointNDF, a denoising framework that combines patch-level geometric context with local displacement prediction. Specifically, a Point Transformer V3 (PTv3) encoder aggregates multiscale geometric information into a global patch descriptor. Rather than directly regressing an unconstrained displacement vector, a Neural Displacement Field (NDF) fuses this global patch descriptor with per-point neighborhood features. It then predicts each displacement through bounded-vector and scale factor branches, thereby achieving a superior, more uniform point distribution. Three cascaded NDF stages propagate local features and progressively refine the point positions. Experiments on PU-Net and ModelNet10 demonstrate competitive denoising accuracy and favorable inference efficiency. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PointNDF, a point cloud denoising framework that combines patch-level geometric context from a Point Transformer V3 encoder with a Neural Displacement Field refined over three cascaded stages. It reports competitive denoising accuracy and favorable inference efficiency on PU-Net and ModelNet10.
AI.motivation: Two-stage denoising methods that regress point displacements with simple regressions lack robust feature guidance and distribution-aware refinement, so they struggle to keep points uniform and preserve geometric quality.
AI.method: A PTv3 encoder aggregates multiscale geometry into a global patch descriptor. A Neural Displacement Field fuses this descriptor with per-point neighborhood features and predicts displacements through bounded-vector and scale-factor branches, with three cascaded NDF stages refining point positions progressively.
AI.result: Experiments on PU-Net and ModelNet10 show competitive denoising accuracy and favorable inference efficiency. The abstract gives no specific metric values.
AI.conclusion: Bounded, distribution-aware displacement prediction over patch context yields a more uniform point distribution than unconstrained regression.

title: SO(3)-Equivariant Learning on CAD Boundary Representations
summary: Learning on boundary representations (B-reps) requires robustness to the pose of a part, since CAD models are not stored in a canonical orientation. Existing B-rep networks either operate on world-frame coordinates and normals, and thus degrade under rotation, or encode each face in a local reference frame. Local frames yield invariance, but reduce inter-face messages to scalars and discard the relative orientation of adjacent faces. We propose SO3brep, an SO(3)-equivariant graph neural network on the B-rep face-adjacency graph. Node features are computed in local frames and mapped into a shared frame by Wigner D-matrices. Clebsch-Gordan tensor products couple these features with the directions between adjacent faces, so that relative orientation is preserved throughout message passing and the output remains SE(3)-invariant. Across three face-segmentation and two classification benchmarks with randomly rotated test parts, SO3brep achieves the highest accuracy among the compared B-rep networks and equivariant point cloud networks, with the fewest parameters. Its advantage is largest with few labeled parts, a setting typical of industrial CAD. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SO3brep, an SO(3)-equivariant graph neural network on the B-rep face-adjacency graph for CAD models. It preserves relative orientation between adjacent faces, and it achieves the highest accuracy among compared B-rep and equivariant point cloud networks with the fewest parameters on randomly rotated test parts.
AI.motivation: CAD models are not stored in a canonical orientation, and existing B-rep networks either degrade under rotation or use local face frames that reduce inter-face messages to scalars and discard relative face orientation.
AI.method: Node features are computed in local face frames and mapped into a shared frame by Wigner D-matrices. Clebsch-Gordan tensor products couple these features with directions between adjacent faces, so relative orientation is kept during message passing and the output stays SE(3)-invariant.
AI.result: Across three face-segmentation and two classification benchmarks with randomly rotated test parts, SO3brep achieves the highest accuracy among the compared methods. It uses the fewest parameters, and its advantage is largest with few labeled parts.
AI.conclusion: Equivariant message passing that retains relative face orientation is useful for industrial CAD learning, especially when labeled data is scarce.

title: From Tokens to Trajectories: Parameter-Efficient Continuous Adaptation of Unified Multimodal Models
summary: While discrete tokenization in Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) establishes strong semantic reasoning, it introduces a strict quantization bottleneck that degrades fine-grained visual details, often resulting in structurally accurate but artifact-heavy images. We introduce FlowShift, a parameter-efficient post-training framework that bypasses this bottleneck by converting pre-trained discrete UMMs into continuous rectified-flow generators. Instead of discarding the backbone's semantic priors, FlowShift replaces discrete visual interfaces with continuous latent projections and applies LoRA to the attention layers. To efficiently boost visual quality without semantic drift, we propose Dual-Objective Velocity Vector Distillation (DOVD), which aligns the model with a high-fidelity continuous teacher and ground-truth continuous trajectories. This approach drastically improves perceptual quality while preserving prompt adherence and reasoning. When applied to leading discrete UMMs, FlowShift significantly improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores, while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities. Ablations confirm DOVD drives generation quality. Ultimately, FlowShift achieves high-fidelity continuous generation without sacrificing pre-trained semantic grounding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FlowShift, a parameter-efficient post-training framework that converts pretrained discrete Unified Multimodal Models into continuous rectified-flow generators. It uses LoRA on attention layers and Dual-Objective Velocity Vector Distillation (DOVD), and it improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding.
AI.motivation: Discrete visual tokenization in UMMs creates a quantization bottleneck that degrades fine-grained detail, which produces structurally accurate but artifact-heavy images.
AI.method: FlowShift replaces discrete visual interfaces with continuous latent projections and applies LoRA to the attention layers, keeping the backbone's semantic priors. DOVD aligns the model with a high-fidelity continuous teacher and with ground-truth continuous trajectories.
AI.result: When applied to leading discrete UMMs, FlowShift significantly improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores, while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities. Ablations confirm that DOVD drives the generation quality gains.
AI.conclusion: Continuous generation can be added to pretrained discrete UMMs without sacrificing their pretrained semantic grounding or prompt adherence.

title: From Activation to Intervention: Interpreting Sparse Visual Features through Reconstruction
comment: Demo and code available at this https URL
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose visual representations into individual features, offering a promising basis for explaining model behavior. Interpreting these features typically relies on images or pixel regions that most strongly activate them. However, this evidence becomes ambiguous when multiple features with different semantics frequently activate in the same locations, such as texture and color in the same patterns. We propose Reconstructive SAE Intervention (RecSAEI), a framework that shifts feature explanation from passive observation to active visual reconstruction. By intervening on representations along SAE decoder directions and reconstructing the visual output, we provide direct evidence of a feature's semantic meaning. We demonstrate that our method successfully disambiguates feature meanings across multiple datasets and vision encoders. Furthermore, our framework grounds [CLS] SAE interventions in a sparse set of patch SAE decoder directions. Beyond stable target response, this attribution also exposes the compositional relationship between elementary visual patterns and high-level semantics. Our results advocate for intervention reconstruction as an essential complementary signal for explaining neural networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RecSAEI, which explains sparse autoencoder visual features by intervening on representations along SAE decoder directions and reconstructing the image. This direct visual evidence disambiguates feature meanings across multiple datasets and vision encoders.
AI.motivation: Explaining SAE features from the images or pixel regions that most strongly activate them is ambiguous when several features with different semantics activate in the same locations, such as texture and color.
AI.method: The framework shifts explanation from passive observation to active visual reconstruction. It intervenes on representations along SAE decoder directions and reconstructs the visual output, and it grounds [CLS] SAE interventions in a sparse set of patch SAE decoder directions.
AI.result: The method disambiguates feature meanings across multiple datasets and vision encoders. The attribution also exposes the compositional relationship between elementary visual patterns and high-level semantics.
AI.conclusion: Intervention-based reconstruction is an essential complementary signal for explaining neural network representations.

title: Lesion Overlap Ranks PET Segmentation Models but Does Not Certify Patient-Level Tumor Burden
summary: Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) summarizes whole-body PET disease burden for prognostic stratification and treatment assessment. Automated MTV is useful only if its estimate is reliable for the individual patient, yet segmentation models are usually evaluated with overlap metrics such as Dice rather than burden error. We examined whether overlap metrics identify unreliable MTV estimates using 1,014 autoPET FDG PET/CT studies. We evaluated LesionTracer predictions held out from fine-tuning, compared five selected released models on 489 tumor-positive patients, and examined the findings in 597 PSMA studies. Across the five FDG models, ranking by higher mean Dice gave the same order as ranking by lower mean relative MTV error ($\rho=-1.00$, exact $p=0.017$). At the patient level, however, out-of-fold Dice tracked relative MTV error strongly ($\rho=-0.75$), yet 82 of 489 patients (16.8\%) fell on opposite sides of the Dice 0.80 and MTV-error 25\% thresholds. Within the training-exposed released models, correlations ranged from $-0.47$ to $-0.74$ over narrower, high-Dice ranges. Out of fold, opposing false-positive and false-negative volumes cancelled about one third of spatial error in net MTV. In 236 of 489 patients, each of the five models missed at least one lesion, though not necessarily the same lesion. Thus, agreement in average model rankings did not establish the reliability of individual MTV estimates or reveal shared lesion misses. PET segmentation benchmarks should report patient-level MTV error and missed-lesion counts alongside Dice and other overlap metrics.

AI.tldr: Using 1,014 autoPET FDG PET/CT studies, the paper shows that model rankings by mean Dice match rankings by mean relative metabolic tumor volume error, but Dice does not reliably certify patient-level tumor burden. It recommends that PET segmentation benchmarks report patient-level MTV error and missed-lesion counts alongside Dice.
AI.motivation: Automated MTV is useful only if reliable for each patient, yet segmentation models are usually evaluated with overlap metrics such as Dice rather than burden error.
AI.method: The authors evaluated LesionTracer predictions held out from fine-tuning, compared five selected released FDG models on 489 tumor-positive patients, and examined findings in 597 PSMA studies. They analyzed rank correlations between Dice and relative MTV error, threshold disagreements, cancellation of spatial error in net MTV, and missed lesions.
AI.result: Across the five FDG models, ranking by higher mean Dice matched ranking by lower mean relative MTV error (rho = -1.00). At patient level, out-of-fold Dice tracked relative MTV error (rho = -0.75), but 82 of 489 patients (16.8%) fell on opposite sides of the Dice 0.80 and MTV-error 25% thresholds. In 236 of 489 patients, each of the five models missed at least one lesion.
AI.conclusion: Agreement in average rankings does not establish the reliability of individual MTV estimates or reveal shared lesion misses, so benchmarks need patient-level burden error and missed-lesion reporting.

title: Role-based Effectiveness of an Epistemic Uncertainty Estimate in Training Models for Semantic Segmentation of 3D LiDAR Point Clouds
summary: Point cloud segmentation is a fundamental task in 3D data analysis, with applications across robotics, augmented and virtual reality, and remote sensing. However, the inherent sparsity, noise, and unordered nature of point clouds introduce significant challenges, particularly in achieving reliable classification. While the state-of-the-art rely on training models for explicit modeling of uncertainty, there is a gap in exploring different roles that estimated uncertainty using generative approaches can play. This work investigates the impact of deterministic uncertainty in point cloud segmentation by explicitly modeling epistemic uncertainty and using it in different roles, namely, as a feature and in loss function. We evaluate a baseline artificial neural network (ANN) and two uncertainty-aware variants (uncertainty as an additional input feature and as a per-sample confidence weight in the training loss) on four large-scale LiDAR benchmarks spanning airborne and mobile acquisition, namely ISPRS Vaihingen, AHN3, Paris-Lille-3D, and Toronto-3D, together with PointNet++ and RandLA-Net references and their uncertainty-augmented counterparts under canonical spatially disjoint train and test splits. Under this protocol, uncertainty-aware modeling improves mean Intersection over Union, recovers minority classes that the baseline ANN never predicts at all, and in half of the configurations improves the alignment between prediction error and estimated uncertainty as measured by Patch Accuracy versus Patch Uncertainty. Our findings indicate that uncertainty can play multiple roles in the segmentation pipeline rather than as a device for improving accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how epistemic uncertainty estimated with a generative approach can be used in point cloud segmentation, either as an extra input feature or as a per-sample confidence weight in the loss. Across four large LiDAR benchmarks, uncertainty-aware modeling improves mean IoU and recovers minority classes the baseline never predicts.
AI.motivation: Prior work trains models to model uncertainty explicitly but does not explore the different roles that estimated uncertainty could play in the segmentation pipeline.
AI.method: The authors compare a baseline ANN with two uncertainty-aware variants, uncertainty as an additional input feature and uncertainty as a per-sample confidence weight in the training loss. They also test PointNet++ and RandLA-Net and their uncertainty-augmented versions on ISPRS Vaihingen, AHN3, Paris-Lille-3D and Toronto-3D under spatially disjoint splits.
AI.result: Uncertainty-aware modeling improves mean IoU and recovers minority classes that the baseline ANN never predicts. In half of the configurations it improves the alignment between prediction error and estimated uncertainty, measured by Patch Accuracy versus Patch Uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty can play multiple roles in segmentation beyond improving accuracy alone.

title: ChangeJEPA: Predict Before You Compare for Remote Sensing Change Detection
summary: Remote sensing change detection is typically formulated as Siamese feature comparison, where two images are encoded independently and a decoder determines which discrepancies correspond to meaningful change. This is challenging because the encoders preserve both true scene changes and nuisance variations such as illumination, seasonal, radiometric, and geometric differences. We introduce ChangeJEPA, a bitemporal joint-embedding predictive architecture that reformulates change detection as latent post-state prediction. Given a pre-change image and partial post-change evidence, ChangeJEPA predicts the full post-change representation under two complementary conditions: a prior hypothesis derived from the pre-change scene and an updated hypothesis conditioned on observed post-change context. A joint-embedding predictive loss aligns both hypotheses with the target latent representation, encouraging semantic consistency while suppressing transient appearance variations. Change is then inferred from the disagreement among the pre-change representation, the observed post-change target, and the predicted latent states, capturing complementary evidence of change, prior surprise, contextual update, and prediction reliability. Across SYSU-CD, LEVIR-CD+, and CDD, ChangeJEPA consistently outperforms its decoder matched Siamese baseline by up to 1.51 IoU points and achieves the best IoU and F1-score on all three benchmarks, demonstrating the advantage of latent post-state prediction over direct feature comparison. Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: ChangeJEPA reformulates remote sensing change detection as latent post-state prediction with a bitemporal joint-embedding predictive architecture, and infers change from disagreement among latent representations. It outperforms its decoder-matched Siamese baseline by up to 1.51 IoU points and gives the best IoU and F1 on SYSU-CD, LEVIR-CD+ and CDD.
AI.motivation: Siamese feature comparison struggles because encoders preserve nuisance variations such as illumination, season, radiometry and geometry alongside true scene changes.
AI.method: Given a pre-change image and partial post-change evidence, ChangeJEPA predicts the full post-change representation under a prior hypothesis from the pre-change scene and an updated hypothesis conditioned on observed post-change context. A joint-embedding predictive loss aligns both hypotheses with the target latent, and change is read from disagreement among the pre-change, observed post-change and predicted latent states.
AI.result: ChangeJEPA consistently outperforms its decoder-matched Siamese baseline by up to 1.51 IoU points. It achieves the best IoU and F1-score on SYSU-CD, LEVIR-CD+ and CDD.
AI.conclusion: Predicting the latent post-state is more advantageous than direct feature comparison for change detection, since it suppresses transient appearance variation.

title: Whose Values Are Generated? Measuring Visual Value Leakage in Multilingual Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) systems serve users across languages and cultural contexts. However, evaluations of cultural representation focus mainly on recognizable elements such as landmarks, clothing, and activities, overlooking the cultural values that generated images convey. To bridge this gap, we introduce VisionValueBench, a multilingual benchmark that operationalizes six of Hofstede's cultural value dimensions (e.g., individualism versus collectivism) to investigate how T2I systems frame neutral social situations through a particular cultural orientation. We find that value-neutral prompts, which admit diverse cultural interpretations, nonetheless yield images that favor particular value orientations, a phenomenon we call visual value leakage. We evaluate prompts varying in language and geographic cues across 960 social scenarios and six T2I configurations. Generated images consistently favor the same value orientations across all six dimensions, for example, equality over hierarchy (low power distance), individual autonomy over group obligation (individualism), and enjoyment over restraint (indulgence). Prompt language has limited influence on these orientations, whereas geographic cues shift some dimensions toward the associated cultural values while largely preserving the prevailing orientations. These findings reveal substantial homogeneity in the cultural values conveyed by T2I systems worldwide.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VisionValueBench, a multilingual benchmark built on six of Hofstede's cultural value dimensions, and finds that text-to-image systems give value-neutral prompts images that favor particular value orientations, a phenomenon called visual value leakage. Prompt language has limited influence, while geographic cues shift some dimensions.
AI.motivation: Evaluations of cultural representation in text-to-image systems focus on recognizable elements such as landmarks, clothing and activities, and overlook the cultural values that generated images convey.
AI.method: The authors evaluate prompts that vary in language and geographic cues across 960 social scenarios and six T2I configurations, operationalizing six Hofstede value dimensions such as individualism versus collectivism.
AI.result: Generated images consistently favor the same value orientations across all six dimensions, for example equality over hierarchy, individual autonomy over group obligation, and enjoyment over restraint. Prompt language has limited influence on these orientations, whereas geographic cues shift some dimensions toward associated cultural values while largely preserving the prevailing orientations.
AI.conclusion: T2I systems convey substantial homogeneity in cultural values worldwide, which the benchmark makes measurable.

title: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats
comment: Under review at TMLR. 32 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: this https URL

AI.tldr: GaussianRenderFormer is a transformer that renders 3D Gaussian splats directly into images without a rasterizer, treating each Gaussian as a token. It renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a neural network can learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, without a rasterizer in the renderer.
AI.method: A view-independent encoder takes one token per Gaussian, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. The model is trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each.
AI.result: On 300 unseen objects, GaussianRenderFormer reaches 38.08 dB PSNR against the full unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. Telling the decoder the projected footprint of each Gaussian adds 1.4 dB.
AI.conclusion: The gap appears to be a bottleneck in the view decoder rather than a generalization failure, though the authors do not rule out under-training.

title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
summary: Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches 0.565 mean intersection over union (mIoU) against 0.502. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

AI.tldr: CAPTOR estimates a term-by-patch grounding matrix without a text encoder by clustering a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and counting caption co-occurrence. It leads training-free baselines on COCO, VOC and Cityscapes and exceeds baselines that use a pathology text encoder on held-out breast-cancer slides.
AI.motivation: Grounding text in images normally needs an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology models trained on slides alone, lack.
AI.method: CAPTOR clusters a frozen encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of these shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest, so the matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor.
AI.result: On COCO, scored on cells one object owns, CAPTOR reaches 0.565 mIoU against 0.502 for the strongest training-free baseline. On held-out breast-cancer slides it exceeds the strongest pathology text-encoder baseline by 0.160 mIoU, and UNI exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid.
AI.conclusion: Counting caption co-occurrence can give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

title: ARIDA - Active railway infrastructure dataset annotation using neural network predictions
summary: Modern railway perception requires large comprehensive image datasets, but creating them is slowed by manual labeling, especially for track polylines and other complex infrastructure geometry. This paper presents the Active Railway Infrastructure Dataset Annotation framework, a railway-specific semi-automated pipeline that converts instance predictions from a mask scoring instance segmentation network into bounding-boxes, polygons, polylines, and paired polylines. To keep automatic track geometry annotation reliable without ground truth, it applies confidence thresholds and an unique contour-agreement quality score as an acceptance gate. An active learning loop ranks remaining images by uncertainty and adapts the number of manual queries per cycle. This is achieved through a novel quantity control mechanism, in which easy images are auto-accepted and human effort targets hard cases. Experiments on disjoint, diverse imagery and time-sequential, redundant imagery quantify effort reduction and accuracy trade-offs, achieving about two thirds reduction in the disjoint regime and up to 93% in the sequential regime. The study also provides guidance for initial label budgets and stopping to avoid over-annotation.

AI.tldr: ARIDA is a railway-specific semi-automated annotation pipeline that converts instance predictions from a mask scoring segmentation network into boxes, polygons, polylines and paired polylines, using an active learning loop. It reports about two-thirds effort reduction on disjoint imagery and up to 93% on time-sequential imagery.
AI.motivation: Railway perception needs large image datasets, but manual labeling is slow, especially for track polylines and other complex infrastructure geometry.
AI.method: A contour-agreement quality score and confidence thresholds act as an acceptance gate for automatic annotations without ground truth. An active learning loop ranks remaining images by uncertainty and adapts the number of manual queries per cycle, auto-accepting easy images and directing human effort to hard cases.
AI.result: Experiments on disjoint, diverse imagery show about two-thirds reduction in effort, and on time-sequential, redundant imagery the reduction reaches up to 93%. The study quantifies accuracy trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The study gives guidance on initial label budgets and stopping criteria to avoid over-annotation.

title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
summary: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

AI.tldr: NitroFusion2 adds Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which uses intermediate text-token states of multimodal diffusion transformers as the adversarial representation, and Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD). It reduces few-step distillation from 4 to 8 steps down to 1 to 2 steps at comparable quality.
AI.motivation: Adversarial diffusion distillation has relied on image features for discrimination, but in multimodal diffusion transformers the text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention and could serve as a discriminative signal.
AI.method: TSAD uses text-token states as a new adversarial representation, and ACD conditions the discriminator on aspects such as typography, objects or style to steer which properties are emphasized. These are integrated with the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion.
AI.result: At one step, NitroFusion2 produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details. At two steps it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The MMDiT text stream is a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
summary: Background: The automatic identification of tree species from bark photographs is of practical interest for forestry inventory and the wood-processing industry, yet the design choices that govern the accuracy of deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some prior results may be inflated by leakage of images of the same trunk across training and test partitions. Methods: A systematic ablation study is conducted on the public BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species) under the established tree-level, leakage-safe partitioning scheme. Using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones, the following factors are varied in turn and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation: patch size, the strategy by which per-patch predictions are aggregated into an image-level decision, the training regime (single- versus two-stage), backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and the number of patches available at inference. Results: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically with patch size (from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px), and image-level accuracy rises in step, plateauing near 94.9% around 512 px. Learned aggregation exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp, an advantage that shrinks as patches grow and attention becomes near-uniform. Backbone capacity (pico to tiny) alters accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training offers no advantage over one-stage. Whole-image classification (91.9%) trails patch-based aggregation, since it admits no bag to average over; accuracy increases with the number of patches at inference, saturating around 64. Conclusions: The study yields a simple recommended configuration: patches as large as possible while leaving enough to average over (around 512 px here), with a nano backbone. It also quantifies the second-order role of learned aggregation and model capacity, providing a reproducible reference point for practitioners and future research

AI.tldr: A leakage-safe ablation on the BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species) with ConvNeXt-V2 backbones finds that larger patches help most, with image-level accuracy near 94.9% around 512 px, and that backbone capacity and two-stage training matter little. The authors recommend the largest patches that leave enough to average over, with a nano backbone.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning design choices for bark-based tree species identification have not been studied systematically, and some prior results may be inflated by leakage of the same trunk across partitions.
AI.method: Under tree-level leakage-safe partitioning with five-fold cross-validation, the authors vary patch size, the aggregation strategy from patch predictions to an image decision, single- versus two-stage training, backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and the number of patches at inference.
AI.result: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically with patch size, from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px, and image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% around 512 px. Learned aggregation exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp, whole-image classification reaches 91.9%, and accuracy saturates around 64 patches.
AI.conclusion: The study yields a simple recommended configuration, with patches as large as possible while leaving enough to average over, and it provides a reproducible reference point for practitioners.

title: TRUST-Stereo: Teacher-Assisted Robust Uncertainty-Guided Search and Transfer for Fast Stereo Matching
summary: Coarse-to-fine stereo matching enables efficient disparity estimation but remains sensitive to errors in propagated disparity, which may place ground-truth correspondences outside subsequent local search ranges. We propose TRUST-Stereo (Teacher-Assisted Robust Uncertainty-Guided Search and Transfer for Fast Stereo Matching), which addresses this limitation through an Uncertainty-Guided Residual Search Module (UGRSM). UGRSM estimates the reliability of propagated disparity and predicts residual offsets to adaptively relocate local cost-volume centers. Additionally, we introduce a two-stage Senior-Junior Teacher Assistant knowledge distillation strategy to transfer rich monocular representations from a large foundation model to a lightweight backbone to achieve fast stereo matching performance. Experiments on KITTI 2012, KITTI 2015, ETH3D, and Middlebury demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization. Using only 1.4M synthetic stereo pairs, TRUST-Stereo achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark metrics, outperforming competing efficient methods trained with substantially larger datasets, including real-world pseudo-labeled samples. Specifically, it achieves a KITTI 2015 EPE of 0.93, ETH3D Bad 1.0 of 2.13% and Middlebury Bad 2.0 of 6.79% while maintaining inference at approximately 50 ms per stereo pair.

AI.tldr: TRUST-Stereo is a fast coarse-to-fine stereo matcher with an Uncertainty-Guided Residual Search Module that relocates cost-volume centers, and a two-stage Senior-Junior Teacher Assistant distillation from a monocular foundation model. Trained on 1.4M synthetic stereo pairs, it reaches state-of-the-art results on several benchmark metrics at about 50 ms per pair.
AI.motivation: Coarse-to-fine stereo matching is sensitive to errors in propagated disparity, which can place ground-truth correspondences outside the local search range.
AI.method: UGRSM estimates the reliability of propagated disparity and predicts residual offsets to adaptively relocate local cost-volume centers. A two-stage Senior-Junior Teacher Assistant distillation transfers monocular representations from a large foundation model to a lightweight backbone.
AI.result: The method reaches a KITTI 2015 EPE of 0.93, an ETH3D Bad 1.0 of 2.13% and a Middlebury Bad 2.0 of 6.79%, with inference at about 50 ms per stereo pair. It outperforms competing efficient methods trained on larger datasets, including real-world pseudo-labeled samples.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-guided search and teacher-assisted distillation give strong zero-shot generalization with a small synthetic training set.

title: Anchored Slice Propagation with Boundary Transport for 3D CT Segmentation from Three Orthogonal Annotated Slices
summary: Sli2Vol propagates a binary mask through affinities between adjacent slices, but an error can persist because each prediction becomes the input to the next step. Three orthogonal annotations reduce dependence on any one chain, yet they offer more than three starting masks: where a chain crosses another annotated plane, the correct label is already known. Those labels could correct drift during propagation and indicate how much to trust each chain at fusion. Between annotated planes, the information carried by the chain may matter as well. A binary mask records foreground membership but discards distance to the boundary, a cue that could help follow gradual shape changes between this http URL address these two sources of error with a fixed pretrained affinity backbone. We anchor each chain by correcting its prediction where it crosses another annotated plane, then use its agreement with those labels to weight fusion. We compare this anchored mask with two ways of transporting boundary geometry: a truncated signed-distance field (SDF) propagated by dense affinity averaging, and a contour whose vertices follow motion cues from the same affinity. The contour tracker starts from a hand-crafted rule and learns a motion correction from supervoxel pseudo-objects in 506 CT volumes, without manual organ labels. On 2,091 held-out structure instances from approximately 403 CT scans spanning 17 abdominal structures, anchoring raises mean Dice from 0.737 with orthogonal mask propagation to 0.769 and improves every structure. Beyond the anchored mask, learned contour tracking improves Dice by 5.7\% for the esophagus and 5.9\% for the postcava, while SDF transport improves right-adrenal Dice by 2.8\%. The anchored methods have similar mean Dice (0.769--0.772); contour tracking performs worse on the kidneys, stomach, and hepatic vessel tree.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes anchored slice propagation for 3D CT segmentation from three orthogonal annotated slices, correcting each propagation chain where it crosses another annotated plane and weighting fusion by agreement. Mean Dice rises from 0.737 with orthogonal mask propagation to 0.769 across 17 abdominal structures.
AI.motivation: Sli2Vol propagates masks through adjacent-slice affinities, so errors persist along each chain. A binary mask also discards distance to the boundary, which could help track gradual shape changes between annotated planes.
AI.method: Each chain is corrected at crossings with other annotated planes, and its agreement with those labels weights fusion. The authors compare an anchored mask with a truncated signed-distance field transported by dense affinity averaging, and with a contour whose vertices follow learned motion corrections trained on supervoxel pseudo-objects in 506 CT volumes.
AI.result: On 2,091 held-out structure instances from about 403 CT scans, anchoring raises mean Dice from 0.737 to 0.769 and improves every structure. Learned contour tracking improves Dice by 5.7% for the esophagus and 5.9% for the postcava, and SDF transport improves right-adrenal Dice by 2.8%. Contour tracking performs worse on the kidneys, stomach and hepatic vessel tree.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring is the main gain, and the anchored variants reach similar mean Dice of 0.769 to 0.772, with boundary transport helping only some structures.

title: GeoDIVE: Geospatial Descent Informed by Value Estimation
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material
summary: Finding specific objects, structures, and spatial patterns supports critical work in agriculture, infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. These features, however, are often dispersed across very large regions and span dramatically different spatial scales, which defines a search space that is costly to embed, maintain, and search naively. We introduce GeoDIVE, a model that treats a multiresolution satellite image gallery as a forest and uses best-first traversal to determine which tiles to encode. At each visited node, a lightweight model then predicts an optimistic estimate of the best query similarity hidden among its descendants using the query and subtree representations. In evaluations with image and open-vocabulary text queries, GeoDIVE matches exhaustive search at 10% of the encoding cost for image queries and leads all tested baselines at every budget in both modalities. To support future evaluation of multiscale geospatial search, we also release object-level image and text queries for Git-10M, constructed from Microsoft building footprints and OpenStreetMap polygons with VLM-generated captions. Source code and models will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: GeoDIVE treats a multiresolution satellite image gallery as a forest and uses best-first traversal to decide which tiles to encode for open-vocabulary and image-based geospatial search.
